name: Garnet
workload: RESP-translated YCSB-A workload, 256M 8-byte keys, string values 8B-several KB, using memtier_benchmark and Garnet's own Resp.bench load generator against Garnet/Valkey/KeyDB/Dragonfly on Azure Standard F72s_v2 VMs (72 vCPUs, 144GB RAM), Ubuntu 24.04, accelerated TCP networking
claimed_speedup: Table 1 (normalized to Redis; the paper says Redis performs like Valkey and leaves it out of most runs, so the measured comparisons are against Valkey v8.1): node throughput 108x, latency at batch size 16 0.25x (4x lower), checkpoint speed 257x (Valkey 273.1s vs Garnet 1.06s), scale-out/migration speed 94x vs Valkey; memtier (1:9 SET:GET, 256M keys, 6400 clients): at least 20x higher throughput and 3x lower P99 latency than standalone Valkey, up to 40x/6x higher throughput than KeyDB/Dragonfly
hardware: Azure Standard F72s_v2 VMs, 72 vCPUs, 144GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04 with accelerated TCP networking
stars_or_usage: 12k stars; the paper says Garnet is 'already widely deployed in large-scale scenarios across Microsoft'
tradeoffs: Runs on the .NET runtime (GC, JIT) rather than being a native binary; kernel-bypass networking (eRPC/DPDK path) used for the best latency numbers is a prototype not shipped in the open-source build; complex RESP data types (SortedSet, HyperLogLog) add overhead
caveats: Evaluation run and published by Garnet's own authors (all seven are Microsoft Research); the paper is peer-reviewed (PVLDB 19(2):224-237) but is not independent. Redis itself was mostly not run: the paper says open-source Redis performs like Valkey and uses Valkey v8.1 (plus KeyDB v6.3.4 and Dragonfly v1.29.0) as the measured baselines, so the 'normalized to Redis' ratios stand in for Redis. The CPU model is not given (only the Azure F72s_v2 SKU), and the .NET runtime version and build flags are not stated. memtier_benchmark became client-bottlenecked, so most headline figures come from Garnet's own Resp.bench tool. Language is C#, not C++.
found_via: GitHub: microsoft/FASTER README (deprecated, points to Garnet as successor) -> gh api repos/microsoft/garnet; VLDB paper fetched via WebFetch from https://badrish.net/papers/garnet-vldb2026.pdf and read as PDF

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed PVLDB 19(2):224-237 paper; Table 1 (normalized to Redis) and Sec. 8 give 108x throughput, 0.25x latency, 257x checkpoint and 94x scale-out, and the load generator is public (benchmark/Resp.benchmark in the repo). It is not A because the paper names only the Azure VM SKU (F72s_v2), with no CPU model and no .NET/compiler version or flags.
verification.notes: The record's caveat claiming Facebook/Meta-adjacent academic co-authors was wrong: all authors are Microsoft Research, and I corrected it. The measured baseline is Valkey v8.1 (a Redis fork) acting as the Redis proxy. The C++-only search filter returned a C# project.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Table 1 (normalized to Redis): node throughput 108x, P99 latency at batch size 16 down to 0.25x; memtier GET throughput >=20x higher and P99 latency 3x lower than Valkey at high client load; up to 40x/6x higher throughput than KeyDB/Dragonfly in some GET experiments; checkpoint speed 257x, scale-out (migration) speed 94x vs Redis
corrected_fields.stars_or_usage: 12k stars; described as widely deployed inside Microsoft
corrected_fields.caveats: Evaluation performed and published by Garnet's own authors (Microsoft Research + Facebook/Meta-adjacent academics via VLDB peer review), not a fully independent third party, though it is peer-reviewed (PVLDB 19(2):224-237) with full hardware/workload disclosure; memtier_benchmark itself became client-bottlenecked at high throughput so most headline figures use Garnet's own Resp.bench tool instead

name: AdaptSize
baseline: LRU (via unmodified Varnish Cache, a concurrent-LRU CDN memory cache with no admission control)
workload: Production CDN edge-cache trace replay comparing an unmodified Varnish Cache deployment against Varnish patched with the AdaptSize size-and-popularity-aware admission policy
claimed_speedup: Object hit ratio (OHR) improves by 47-91% over unmodified Varnish (+47% on the HK trace, +91% on the US trace) and by 30-48% over offline-tuned Nginx, with a 1.2 GiB hot object cache. OHR variability (coefficient of variation) improves by 1.9x on HK and 3.8x on US. Throughput is indistinguishable from unmodified Varnish: both peak at 17.5 Gb/s at 50 client threads in the 100%-hit case, and the 0%-hit case stays within the 95% confidence interval.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.4.7 (specific optimization flags not stated)
hardware: FUJITSU CX250 HPC servers, dual Intel Xeon E5-2670 CPUs, 32GB RAM, RHEL 6.5 / kernel 2.6.32, IB QDR networking
tradeoffs: Proof-of-concept quality, not production-ready per its own README; admission-only policy (still relies on Varnish's own LRU eviction); needs periodic re-solving of its size-to-admission-probability model
caveats: The win is in hit ratio, not speed: AdaptSize matches Varnish's throughput and does not exceed it. gcc 4.4.7 is stated but optimization flags are not. The prototype comparison uses Akamai production traces, which are not public. The baseline is Varnish's LRU with no admission control (plus tuned Nginx), not a standalone LRU library. The research-policy comparisons (33-46% over research systems) come from a separate single-threaded C++ simulator.
found_via: gh api users/dasebe/repos; gh api repos/dasebe/AdaptSize/readme; NSDI'17 paper PDF

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NSDI'17 paper comparing the AdaptSize-patched Varnish prototype against unmodified Varnish 4.1.2 (LRU, no admission) and tuned Nginx on Akamai production traces. Code is public (github.com/dasebe/AdaptSize) and gcc 4.4.7 on dual Xeon E5-2670 is stated, but optimization flags are not and the Akamai traces are not public, so it falls short of A.
verification.notes: The record's 0.66 vs 0.42 OHR (1.57x) and CoV 5% vs 23% (4.6x) figures appear nowhere in the paper text. The paper states +47-91% over Varnish and a 1.9x/3.8x CoV improvement, so claimed_speedup was replaced. All metadata checks out: BSD-2-Clause, 43 stars, last commit 2018-01-30, not archived or forked.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: AdaptSize achieves a 0.66 hit ratio vs 0.42 for unmodified Varnish (1.57x improvement), and stabilizes hit ratio variability (coefficient of variation 5% vs 23%, a 4.6x improvement), with no added throughput overhead (scales identically to unmodified Varnish)
corrected_fields.caveats: Compiler version is stated (gcc 4.4.7) but exact optimization flags are not, so capped at tier B rather than A; production-trace comparison is against Varnish specifically, not raw textbook LRU or memcached/Redis

name: Cacheus
workload: 17,766 trace-driven simulations over 329 single-day production block-storage workloads from 5 datasets (FIU, MSR, CloudPhysics, CloudVPS, CloudCache) at 6 cache sizes (0.05%-10% of workload footprint), comparing hit rate against LRU, LFU, ARC, LIRS, LeCaR and DLIRS
claimed_speedup: In paired t-tests over 17,766 simulations, Cacheus C3 (SR-LRU + CR-LFU experts) is distinctly the best algorithm in 47% of workload/cache-size combinations, statistically indistinguishable from the best state-of-the-art algorithm in about 40%, and worse in the remaining 13%. The comparison set is LRU, LFU, ARC, LIRS, LeCaR and DLIRS. The best case is a 38.32% absolute hit-rate difference over ARC (CloudPhysics, cache at 10% of footprint). The worst case is a 15.12% degradation vs DLIRS (MSR, cache at 5% of footprint).
license: reference (no LICENSE file found in repo)
tradeoffs: Not uniformly better than every competitor (worst case is a real hit-rate loss vs DLIRS); adaptive combination of multiple experts (ARC/LIRS/LFU-style) adds bookkeeping overhead vs plain LRU; reference Python implementation is a research prototype, not built for production throughput (a C port exists inside libCacheSim)
caveats: This is a pure trace-driven Python simulation with no throughput, latency or hardware numbers, and the win is in hit rate. The paper isolates no Cacheus-vs-LRU number: its headline statistics are against the stronger ARC/LIRS/DLIRS/LeCaR baselines, and LRU appears only in the compared-algorithm set and the ranking study. The repo has no LICENSE file, so it is reference-only for reuse.
found_via: gh search repos 'cacheus'; FAST'21 paper PDF (usenix.org)

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed FAST'21 paper with 17,766 trace-driven simulations. LRU is one of the six algorithms compared, and the quantified Cacheus results are against ARC, LIRS, DLIRS and LeCaR. It is a Python simulation with no compiler or hardware stated, so it cannot reach A.
verification.notes: The numbers 17,766 / 38.32% / 15.12% are on the page. The record's 'majority of paired t-tests' is overstated: the paper says 47% distinctly best, about 40% tie, 13% worse. The workload was also missing 2 of the 5 datasets. Metadata confirmed: no license (null, and the repo root has no LICENSE file), 68 stars, last commit 2023-10-05 (stale, just under 3 years), Python.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Cacheus (using SR-LRU + CR-LFU experts) is statistically significantly better than ARC/LIRS/DLIRS/LeCaR in the majority of paired t-tests across 17,766 experiments; best-case improvement of 38.32% higher hit rate than ARC (CloudPhysics trace, 10% cache size); worst case is a 15.12% hit-rate degradation vs DLIRS (MSR trace, 5% cache size)
corrected_fields.workload: 17,766 simulation experiments over FIU, MSR and CloudPhysics block-storage traces at varying cache sizes, comparing hit rate against ARC, LIRS, DLIRS and LeCaR
corrected_fields.caveats: Pure trace-driven simulation, no throughput/latency numbers or hardware given; repo has no OSI license file so treated as reference-only for reuse

name: Caffeine
workload: JMH microbenchmark (ComputeBenchmark/GetPutBenchmark) at 16 threads, varying read/write mixes (100% read, 75/25 read/write, 100% write) on a bounded in-process cache, vs ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, Guava Cache, Ehcache, Infinispan and plain ConcurrentHashMap
claimed_speedup: Server-class (Xeon E5-2698B v3, 16 threads, bounded caches), GetPutBenchmark: 100% read 382.4M ops/s vs 313.9M (ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, ~1.2x) and 43.1M (Guava with concurrencyLevel 64, ~8.9x) (derived from page data); 75/25 read/write 279.4M vs 122.3M (~2.3x) and 37.3M (Guava-64, ~7.5x) (derived from page data); 100% write 48.3M vs 39.8M (~1.2x) (derived from page data). JDK LinkedHashMap LRU reaches only 13.6M/12.8M/10.9M ops/s in the same runs.
hardware: Server-class: single-socket Xeon E5-2698B v3 @ 2.00GHz, 16 cores (hyperthreading disabled), 224GB RAM, Ubuntu 15.04, Azure G4 instance; desktop-class: MacBook Pro i7-4870HQ @ 2.50GHz
stars_or_usage: 17.9k stars; used as the cache implementation inside Spring, Cassandra, Solr and others
tradeoffs: In-process JVM cache, not a distributed/remote cache like Redis or Memcached, so it solves a different deployment problem (per-process hit ratio and speed rather than shared/networked state); W-TinyLFU admission policy adds bookkeeping vs a plain LRU
caveats: First-party numbers only. The exact JVM version and flags for the JMH run are not given. The server run is an old Azure G4 / Ubuntu 15.04 setup (the desktop run is on OS X Yosemite), so the figures date from roughly 2015 and an early Caffeine release. The Guava ratios use Guava tuned to concurrencyLevel 64; Guava's default does worse. Benchmark code is public (ComputeBenchmark.java, GetPutBenchmark.java under caffeine/src/jmh). Language is Java, not C++.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos --topic cache --language c++ did not surface this; found via reasoning about 'LRU baselines the benchmark names' + gh api repos/ben-manes/caffeine, then WebFetch of the Benchmarks wiki page

verification.tier_reason: First-party wiki page with JMH numbers against ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, Guava, Ehcache, Infinispan and java.util.LinkedHashMap LRU. The code is public (caffeine/src/jmh/.../GetPutBenchmark.java) and the CPU is stated, but the JVM version and flags are not. The rubric makes the project's own benchmark code with partial methodology C, not B; there is no peer-reviewed or independent third-party source.
verification.notes: All the figures match the server-class tables on the wiki; the ratios are computed and are now marked as derived. The C++-only search filter returned a Java project. The rubric's rule that own code with partial methodology is C forced the downgrade from B.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: server-class (Xeon E5-2698B v3, 16 threads): 100% read 382.4M ops/s vs 313.9M (ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, ~1.2x) and 43.1M (Guava, ~8.9x); 75/25 read/write 279.4M vs 122.3M (~2.3x) and 37.3M (Guava, ~7.5x); 100% write 48.3M vs 39.8M (~1.2x)
corrected_fields.caveats: CPU model and OS are stated but the exact JVM version/flags used for the JMH run are not given in the wiki page as fetched; benchmark code and harness are public in the repo (ComputeBenchmark.java, GetPutBenchmark.java) which is why this is scored B rather than C

name: GL-Cache
workload: 118 production traces (103 CloudPhysics block I/O, 14 MSR block I/O, 1 Wikimedia CDN) replayed in a closed loop against a local cache, measuring hit ratio and throughput. Two setups: a prototype built on Pelikan's Segcache, compared against Cachelib (LRU), Segcache, TinyLFU and LHD; and a storage-oblivious C micro-implementation on libCacheSim, compared against FIFO, LRU, size-aware Belady, LHD, LRB and Cacheus.
claimed_speedup: Against LRU the win is hit ratio, not throughput. In the Segcache-based prototype, GL-Cache has the highest hit ratio, up to 40% above the best baseline, while Cachelib's throughput-optimized LRU has the lowest hit ratio of all baselines, at throughput similar to Cachelib and Segcache. In the micro-implementation, LRU improves FIFO's hit ratio only by single-digit percent for the median trace, while GL-Cache improves it much more. On throughput, GL-Cache-E is 228x faster than LRB on average (GL-Cache-T 586x) at the small cache size, and 64% faster than the fastest other learned cache (GL-Cache-T 3x). GL-Cache is not faster than LRU itself: the paper says LRU runs close to FIFO throughput, and GL-Cache-E reaches almost half of FIFO's throughput on the Wikimedia trace.
hardware: Micro-implementation: CloudLab Utah m510 nodes, Intel Xeon D-1548, 64GB ECC DDR4. Prototype: CloudLab Clemson c6420 nodes, Intel Xeon Gold 6142, 384GB DRAM.
tradeoffs: Batches evictions over object groups instead of single objects, trading some eviction precision for far lower learning/inference overhead than object-level learned caches (e.g. LRB)
caveats: Against LRU, GL-Cache wins on hit ratio and is not faster: it runs below LRU/FIFO throughput, so the record's metric 'throughput' does not describe the LRU comparison. The 64% throughput figure is against the fastest other learned cache, not LRB, and the LRB gap is 228x/586x. GL-Cache does not beat size-aware Belady, which is an oracle. The paper's own artifact is github.com/Thesys-lab/fast23-GLCache, which has no license file and was last committed 2023-05-12. The libCacheSim copy is Apache-2.0 but opt-in (-DENABLE_GLCACHE=ON) and depends on XGBoost. Compiler and flags are not stated.
found_via: junchengyang.com publication page; libCacheSim README algorithm list

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed FAST'23 paper that evaluates GL-Cache against LRU (plain LRU in the libCacheSim micro-implementation, Cachelib's LRU in the prototype) on 118 production traces. The code is public and CPU models are stated, but compiler and flags are not, so it falls short of A.
verification.notes: The record misattributed the 64% throughput gain to LRB (the paper says 228x vs LRB) and wrongly said GL-Cache beats size-aware Belady. 'metric' should arguably be hit ratio (other), but that field is not correctable here. Metadata confirmed via gh: libCacheSim Apache-2.0, 347 stars, last commit 2026-09-26, GLCache sources present under libCacheSim/cache/eviction/GLCache with the ENABLE_GLCACHE CMake option. The orchestrator may prefer the Thesys-lab/fast23-GLCache artifact repo as a secondary link.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: GL-Cache achieves 64% higher throughput than LRB (the prior object-level learned cache) at similar hit ratio; paper's evaluation table also reports GL-Cache beating LRU and size-aware Belady baselines directly, though the exact LRU-relative percentage is not isolated in the text we extracted
corrected_fields.workload: Production CDN/KV traces replayed through a Memcached-like prototype on CloudLab, measuring both hit ratio and throughput; group-level (not per-object) learned eviction
corrected_fields.hardware: CloudLab Utah site m510 nodes: Intel Xeon D-1548 and Intel Xeon Gold 6142, 384GB DRAM
corrected_fields.caveats: The clearest quantified comparison in the extracted text is against LRB, not literally against raw LRU/memcached; less exercised code path than the core libCacheSim algorithms (opt-in build flag)

name: Hyperbolic Caching
workload: Django-Wiki and NodeJS web applications using a modified Redis (forked at 3.0) as a look-aside cache, replaying Wikipedia (Jan 2008) and synthetic cost-aware workloads; also Memcachier-style trace-driven miss-rate simulation
claimed_speedup: Hyperbolic caching improves end-to-end application throughput by ~5-10% over default Redis (abstract) and lowers miss rates by 10-37% on the NodeJS synthetic workloads, with throughput up to ~14% higher. Example, Fig. 11 (NodeJS over Redis, Dynamic Intro, 5k-object cache): 10.0 vs 11.3 kreq/s and miss rate 0.33 vs 0.27 for default vs HC Redis (+11.6%). Fig. 7 (Django-Wiki, Wikipedia Jan 2008 trace): 21.1 vs 23.7 req/s (+12.3%) for default vs HC.
hardware: Rack of servers with Intel Xeon E5620 @ 2.40GHz CPUs
tradeoffs: Priority function needs periodic re-scaling/rebalancing as cost or popularity distributions shift; implemented as a ~380-line patch to Redis's existing random-sampling eviction rather than a new data structure, so gains are workload-dependent (competitive with, not always better than, ARC on cost-free workloads)
caveats: This repo is archived. It holds the Python simulator plus the NodeJS and Django benchmark runners (GitHub language: Python), not the Redis patch itself. The paper's 380-line C Redis change (forked at Redis 3.0) lives in a separate repo, github.com/kantai/redis-hyperbolic-caching (BSD-3-Clause, archived, 6 stars, last commit 2017-05-18). Default Redis eviction here means Redis's sampled approximate LRU. The 2021-12-09 date is the archive push, not a commit.
found_via: ATC'17 paper PDF (usenix.org); paper's own code citation to github.com/kantai/hyperbolic-caching

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed USENIX ATC'17 paper compares HC Redis against default Redis. Fig. 11 (NodeJS, Dynamic Intro, 5k objects) shows 10.0 vs 11.3 kreq/s, miss rate 0.33 vs 0.27, +11.6%; Fig. 7 (Django-Wiki) shows 21.1 vs 23.7 req/s (+12.3%). The CPU (Xeon E5620) is stated and the runner code is public, but no compiler or flags are given, so it is not A.
verification.notes: The claim numbers match the paper; 10.0 vs 11.3 is kreq/s on the page, so 'req/ms' was numerically equivalent but not the page's unit. Last commit on the default branch is 2017-07-14, and the repo is not a GitHub fork. The record's language 'C' fits only the separate Redis-prototype repo, since this repo is Python. That field is not correctable here.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Hyperbolic caching (random-sampling-based priority eviction) improves end-to-end application throughput by ~5-10% over default Redis while also lowering miss rate; e.g. NodeJS-over-Redis benchmark: throughput 10.0 vs 11.3 req/ms and miss rate 0.33 vs 0.27 for default vs Hyperbolic Redis (11.6% throughput gain in that run)
corrected_fields.caveats: Repo is archived; GitHub reports its dominant language as Python (benchmark/harness scripts) even though the core change is a small C patch to Redis -- confirmed by the paper's own '380 lines of code' description of the Redis patch

name: LHD (Least Hit Density) / RankCache
workload: Commercial Memcachier and enterprise storage (MSR) traces simulated for hit-rate/space comparisons; RankCache, an LHD-based memcached-derived KV-cache, benchmarked for request throughput at up to 16 threads
claimed_speedup: LHD needs on average 8x less cache space than LRU (and 2-3x less than other proposed policies) to match the same hit rate; RankCache needs no synchronization in the common case, improving request throughput at 16 threads by 8x over LRU and 2x over CLOCK
hardware: Not stated in the extracted paper text for the RankCache throughput experiment
license: MIT (verbatim MIT text, Copyright 2017-2018 Carnegie Mellon University, plus a non-binding request to cite the LHD paper; GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
tradeoffs: LHD's ranking function relies on modeling conditional-probability hit density which needs periodic reclassification/recomputation; the GitHub repo ships only the trace-driven simulator, not the RankCache memcached-based prototype used for the throughput numbers
caveats: The 8x/2x throughput numbers are for RankCache, a separate prototype built on memcached 1.4.33 that is not in this repo. Its own README calls the CMU-CORGI/LHD repo 'simulation code' only, so the throughput claim cannot be reproduced from it. The throughput test ran inside one server with the network bypassed, on a random Zipfian trace with same-size objects. The paper's intro gives a different figure (16x over list-based LRU; 2x over CLOCK at a 90% hit ratio) than the abstract's 8x. The 8x space saving is an average across the Memcachier and MSR traces. MIT license: no patent grant.
found_via: gh search repos 'LHD cache'; NSDI'18 paper PDF (usenix.org)

verification.tier_reason: The peer-reviewed NSDI'18 paper's abstract states LHD needs on average 8x less space than LRU and 2-3x less than recent policies, and that RankCache at 16 threads improves throughput 8x over LRU and 2x over CLOCK. The repo has only the simulator, and the paper gives no CPU model, compiler or flags, so it is not A.
verification.notes: The claim is quoted almost verbatim from the abstract. The metadata (25 stars, last commit 2018-07-23, abandoned, not a fork) checks out. The LICENSE file is standard MIT plus a citation request, so 'copyable' stands.

corrected_fields.license: Custom MIT-style permissive license (Carnegie Mellon University; requests citation of the LHD paper, no patent grant)
corrected_fields.caveats: The 8x/2x throughput-vs-LRU/CLOCK numbers are attributed to RankCache, a separate memcached-based prototype; the released CMU-CORGI/LHD repo is described by its own README as 'simulation code' only, so the throughput claim may not be independently reproducible from this exact repo

name: LRB (Learning Relaxed Belady) / webcachesim2
workload: Simulation (webcachesim2) replaying 6 production CDN traces (Wikipedia 14-day plus 5 from two other CDNs) at a range of cache sizes vs B-LRU, LRU, LRU4, LFUDA, TinyLFU, LeCaR and others. Also a CDN flash-cache prototype built on Apache Traffic Server 8.0.3, replaying the Wikipedia trace with a 1TB cache.
claimed_speedup: Simulations on 6 production CDN traces: LRB reduces WAN traffic by 4-25% vs B-LRU (the LRU-with-Bloom-filter-admission production CDN design), and by over 13% on average across cache sizes. It is robust across traces where LRU4, LFUDA, TinyLFU and LeCaR each win only on some. Prototype, Wikipedia trace, 1TB flash cache, days 12-14: LRB cuts average WAN bandwidth by 44% and p95 bandwidth by 43% vs unmodified Apache Traffic Server 8.0.3, which the paper says approximates FIFO eviction, not LRU.
hardware: 3x Google Cloud n1-standard-64 VMs (64 vCPUs, 240GB DRAM each) acting as client/proxy/origin, 8x375GB local NVMe combined via software RAID
stars_or_usage: 85 stars (companion prototype repo sunnyszy/lrb-prototype has 11 stars)
tradeoffs: Uses an online-trained ML model (~30us per inference) for eviction scoring, adding CPU overhead versus plain LRU (paper measures peak CPU 16% for LRB vs 9% for ATS at max throughput); needs a validation/warmup trace section to tune hyperparameters
caveats: The paper's prototype baseline, unmodified ATS, approximates FIFO eviction, not LRU. Against LRU-family baselines the win is the simulated 4-25% WAN-traffic reduction vs B-LRU. Raw throughput is essentially tied (LRB 11.72 vs ATS 11.66 Gbps), and LRB uses more peak CPU (16% vs 9%); the win is in bandwidth and miss ratio. The CPU model and compiler/flags are not stated. The repo is a GitHub fork of dasebe/webcachesim; the ATS prototype is in a separate repo, sunnyszy/lrb-prototype (Apache-2.0).
found_via: gh api users/sunnyszy/repos; gh search repos 'learning relaxed belady'; NSDI'20 paper PDF

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NSDI'20 paper. The simulations compare LRB against B-LRU, LRU, LFUDA, TinyLFU, LeCaR and others, and the prototype is compared with unmodified ATS. Code is public (webcachesim2 plus lrb-prototype), but only the VM type is given (no CPU model, compiler or flags), so it is not A. Tier stays B; the verdict is a downgrade because the claim misattributes the 44% win to an LRU baseline.
verification.notes: The 44%/43% and 11.72/11.66 Gbps numbers are on the page, but the record wrongly calls ATS LRU-based (the paper says it approximates FIFO). The default branch's last commit is 2023-01-20; 2023-12-18 is only pushed_at. That is more than 3 years ago, so the repo is abandoned. is_fork_of is set to dasebe/webcachesim.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: LRB reduces average WAN bandwidth consumption by 44% and p95 bandwidth by 43% versus unmodified Apache Traffic Server (ATS, an LRU-based cache) at a 1TB flash cache size; simulations also place LRB's byte-miss-ratio ahead of LRU, LFUDA, TinyLFU and LeCaR across a range of cache sizes
corrected_fields.workload: CDN flash-cache prototype (built on Apache Traffic Server) replaying a 14-day Wikipedia production trace with a 1TB cache, plus simulations against LRU/LFUDA/TinyLFU/LeCaR/B-LRU at multiple cache sizes
corrected_fields.caveats: Compiler/flags not stated in the extracted testbed section; throughput itself was essentially tied between LRB and ATS (11.72 vs 11.66 Gbps) -- the win is in bandwidth/miss-ratio, not raw request throughput

name: MemC3
workload: End-to-end test: 95% GET/5% SET YCSB-generated Zipf workload, pre-generated as traces. It is sent from 50 client nodes over 10Gb Ethernet using libmemcached 1.0.7 multi-get (batches of 100 GETs) to MemC3 vs original Memcached 1.4.13, optimized Memcached, and sharded optimized Memcached. Each system gets 1GB of cache space. Separate local tests cover hash-table lookup throughput (single thread and multi-thread) and cache space efficiency and miss ratio (Table 3).
claimed_speedup: Full-system throughput over the network: MemC3 peaks at 4.4 MOPS vs 1.5 MOPS for original Memcached, 'almost 3x' (Fig. 9, 95% GET/5% SET YCSB Zipf workload). The paper says it uses 30% less memory for small key-value pairs, or stores 30% more objects; Table 3 shows cuckoo+CLOCK holding about 40% more 16B-key/32B-value items than Memcached's default chaining+LRU. The core cuckoo hash table alone does 5M lookups/sec per thread and 35M lookups/sec at 12 threads.
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon L5640 @2.27GHz (2x6 cores), 2x12MB L3 cache, 2x16GB DDR SDRAM, 10Gb Ethernet
tradeoffs: CLOCK-based eviction only approximates strict LRU, trading eviction precision for space/concurrency; cuckoo hashing needs load-factor headroom and can hit rare high-latency insert paths near capacity; the repo's own README says the successor project, libcuckoo, is the actively maintained re-engineering of MemC3's hash table
caveats: The paper does not state the compiler or build flags for the MemC3/Memcached server builds; only the bench client Makefile shows gcc -std=gnu99 -O2. The end-to-end numbers use pre-generated YCSB traces, not live YCSB (the scripts are bench/ycsb_workload_gen.sh and bench/ycsb_workload_settings), with clients batching 100 GETs per multi-get. The server CPU is a low-power L5640. The only branch was last committed 2014-06-28 (repo pushed_at is 2017-04-28), and the project is unmaintained.
found_via: GitHub: search 'memc3'; paper confirmed via USENIX NSDI'13 session page and PDF (Fan, Andersen, Kaminsky, 'MemC3: Compact and Concurrent MemCache with Dumber Caching and Smarter Hashing')

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NSDI'13 paper compares MemC3 against stock Memcached 1.4.13: full-system throughput 4.4 MOPS vs 1.5 MOPS (almost 3x, Fig. 9), 30% less memory for small key-value pairs, and a 5M/35M lookups/sec hash table. The CPU is stated (2x Xeon L5640), but the compiler and flags for the server builds are not, so it falls short of A.
verification.notes: The numbers in the record match the paper. The only fixes are that 'up to 3x' is 4.4 vs 1.5 MOPS ('almost 3x'), the paper lists DRAM as DDR SDRAM, not DDR3, and last_commit was the pushed_at date rather than the last commit on master (2014-06-28). License BSD-3-Clause, 156 stars, not archived, not a fork: all confirmed.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Up to 3x the queries-per-second of stock Memcached on the same workload while using about 30% less memory for small key-value pairs (optimistic concurrent cuckoo hashing + CLOCK eviction combined); the core hash table alone reaches 5M lookups/sec at 1 thread and 35M lookups/sec at 12 threads
corrected_fields.workload: Pre-generated YCSB-style key-value workload traces replayed against MemC3 and stock Memcached over the network to measure end-to-end query throughput and memory footprint for small key-value pairs; a separate local microbenchmark measures raw hash-table lookup throughput at 1 and 12 threads
corrected_fields.hardware: 2x Intel Xeon L5640 @2.27GHz (2x6 cores), 2x12MB L3 cache, 2x16GB DDR3 RAM, 10Gb Ethernet
corrected_fields.caveats: Paper does not state compiler or build flags for the throughput/memory numbers, capping this at Tier B rather than A; the repo's own README notes the benchmark uses pre-generated YCSB-style traces rather than live YCSB; project unmaintained since 2017

name: MICA
workload: Network GET/PUT benchmark over UDP with MICA's DPDK kernel-bypass stack and no client-side batching. Item sizes: tiny (8B/8B), small (16B/64B) and large (128B/1024B). Key popularity is uniform or Zipf(0.99), at 50% and 95% GET. The server has 16 cores running 16 partitions (EREW). Compared against custom versions of Memcached (87e2f36), MemC3, Masstree and RAMCloud, all modified to use MICA's network stack, each run at its best core count. The latency test uses original Memcached with the kernel network stack.
claimed_speedup: Tiny items (8B/8B), Fig. 10: MICA reaches 75.5-76.9 Mops on uniform and 65.6-70.5 Mops on skewed workloads. The next-best system (Masstree) tops out at 16.5 Mops; Memcached, MemC3 and RAMCloud stay at or below 6.1 Mops. Paper headline: 4-13.5x faster than the next fastest system, and 10.8x on skewed 50% GET. Against the custom Memcached (ported to MICA's kernel-bypass stack), which gets 0.7-1.3 Mops, MICA is roughly 50-110x faster on tiny items (derived from page data). Latency (Fig. 13, uniform 50% GET, tiny items) vs original kernel-stack Memcached: at a similar ~40 us latency MICA serves 69 Mops, 'more than two orders of magnitude faster than Memcached'. Original Memcached's latency is almost flat, while MICA's varies between 24 and 52 us depending on load.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The repo README requires gcc >= 4.6.0, and src/CMakeLists.txt sets -O9 -msse4.2 -march=corei7 -g.
hardware: Server: dual 8-core Intel Xeon E5-2680 @2.70GHz, 64GiB RAM (32GiB/NUMA node), 20MiB L3/CPU, eight 10Gb Ethernet ports (four Intel X520-T2 dual-port NICs); Clients: two machines with dual 6-core Intel Xeon L5640 @2.27GHz and Intel X520-T2 NICs
license: Apache-2.0 (license text embedded in README; no separate LICENSE file in the repo)
tradeoffs: Requires Intel DPDK, hugepages, and a specific dual-socket/multi-NIC hardware layout to hit peak numbers; UDP-based protocol with no TCP or automatic loss recovery beyond GET/PUT idempotency; partitioned (EREW) design trades flexibility for scalability; cache mode uses a lossy, approximate-LRU hash index by design
caveats: The paper does not state the compiler version or build flags (flags appear only in the repo's CMake files), which is why this is capped at Tier B. The vs-Memcached/MemC3 throughput figures use custom versions of those systems ported to MICA's lightweight network stack, and those modified versions are not in this repo. The paper used DPDK 1.4.1 and the README requires DPDK >= 1.5.0, 2014-era APIs that will not build against modern DPDK without porting. The license (Apache-2.0) is asserted only in README text, with no LICENSE file. master was last committed 2014-03-03; the most recent commit anywhere is on the isca2015 branch (2016-01-18).
found_via: GitHub: search 'MICA key-value store'; paper confirmed via USENIX NSDI'14 session page and PDF (Lim, Han, Andersen, Kaminsky, 'MICA: A Holistic Approach to Fast In-Memory Key-Value Storage')

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NSDI'14 paper benchmarks MICA against Memcached, MemC3, Masstree and RAMCloud (Fig. 10, 13, 14) with the hardware stated. The netbench code and build flags (src/CMakeLists.txt) are in the repo, but the paper does not state the compiler version and the modified baseline versions are not published, so it is not A. The roughly 50-110x gap to Memcached exceeds the 50x cap threshold but is not implausible: it is against a peer-reviewed baseline that the paper shows peaks at 2 cores (Fig. 14), and the headline claim is 4-13.5x over the next-fastest system.
verification.notes: The core throughput numbers match the paper; the vs-Memcached gap is actually much larger than the record's '>10x'. The workload's '8-partition' was wrong (the paper uses 16 partitions), and the latency clause 'more stable' was wrong (Memcached's latency is the flat one). last_commit 2016-01-18 is the isca2015 branch; the default branch is 2014-03-03; both are abandoned. 215 stars, gh license null, README Apache-2.0: all confirmed.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: MICA reaches 65.6-76.9 Mops on tiny items (uniform and skewed); the next-best system (Masstree) tops out at 16.5 Mops, with Memcached/MemC3/RAMCloud all below 6.1 Mops on the same setup (>10x vs Memcached, >4x vs the next-fastest system overall); MICA's end-to-end latency is also lower and more stable as throughput rises versus original Memcached (Fig. 13, uniform 50% GET, tiny items)
corrected_fields.workload: Network GET/PUT benchmark over UDP/DPDK with tiny (8B key/8B value), small (16B/64B), and large (128B/1024B) items, uniform and Zipf(0.99)-skewed key popularity, 50% and 95% GET ratios, on a 16-core/8-partition server vs custom versions of Memcached, MemC3, Masstree, and RAMCloud
corrected_fields.caveats: Paper does not state compiler or build flags for the throughput numbers, which is why this is capped at Tier B instead of A; repository unmodified since 2016 and targets DPDK 1.4.1-era APIs that will not build against modern DPDK without porting; license is only asserted in README text, not a LICENSE file

name: Pelikan / Segcache
workload: NSDI'21 paper evaluation of Segcache (Pelikan's TTL-segmented storage engine) on production-derived cache workloads, scaling to 24 threads, comparing per-object metadata overhead and multi-core throughput scaling vs Memcached's slab allocator
claimed_speedup: NSDI'21 paper: close to 8x speedup over Memcached with 24 threads (Segcache over 70 MQPS vs Memcached 9 MQPS); up to 40% higher throughput than Memcached on a single thread; 5 bytes/object metadata vs Memcached's 56 bytes (91% less); 22-60% less memory than state-of-the-art designs (abstract), up to 60% less vs Memcached, and 42-88% less memory footprint vs Twitter's production PCache (slab) system
hardware: Dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6230R, 384GB DRAM, one 100Gbps NIC (dedicated hosts in Twitter's production fleet); closed-loop trace replay of the storage subsystem only
stars_or_usage: 295 stars (current Rust rewrite); legacy C implementation at github.com/twitter/pelikan has ~2k stars
tradeoffs: TTL-segmented design trades some flexibility (object grouping by expiry) for memory efficiency; original Segcache/legacy Pelikan was C, current pelikan-io/pelikan is a full Rust rewrite so the exact peer-reviewed binary is not what ships today
caveats: Paper numbers are for the original C Segcache module in twitter/pelikan (archived at thesys-lab/segcache), not the current Rust rewrite at pelikan-io/pelikan; the Rust README repeats them as properties of 'the same architecture'. The evaluation covers the storage subsystem only (the networking stack was not modified), uses Twitter production traces, and was run by Twitter/CMU authors. The compiler and flags are not stated. The README's '40-90% vs Pelikan's own slab storage' rounds the paper's 42-88% vs PCache. Language of the current repo is Rust, not C++.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/pelikan-io/pelikan; README opened directly, linking to Segcache blog and NSDI'21 paper page

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NSDI'21 paper (the abstract on the USENIX page and the full PDF) compares Segcache with Memcached 1.6.6: close to 8x speedup at 24 threads (over 70 vs 9 MQPS) and 5 vs 56 bytes of metadata per object. The CPU (dual Xeon Gold 6230R) and code (twitter/pelikan, thesys-lab/segcache) are given but the compiler and flags are not, so it is not A.
verification.notes: The numbers are now verified against the paper PDF (https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi21-yang.pdf) rather than the blog, and hardware is filled in. Tier B holds, but the benchmarked code is the legacy C implementation (twitter/pelikan: 1,957 stars, last commit 2022-10-27), not the Rust repo. The C++-only search filter returned a Rust project.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: ~8x higher throughput than Memcached at 24 threads; 5 bytes/object metadata vs Memcached's 56 bytes, cutting cache memory requirements 22-60% vs other state-of-the-art designs and 40-90% vs Pelikan's own prior slab storage
corrected_fields.caveats: Numbers are quoted from the project's own blog restating its peer-reviewed NSDI'21 paper; did not obtain the paper PDF directly in this session to confirm exact hardware/CPU model and compiler flags used in the formal evaluation, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A

name: Pogocache
workload: memtier_benchmark with 16 client threads x 16 connections (256 connections), each doing 100K SETs then 100K GETs with random 1-1024 B values. The server is pinned to cores 0-15 and configured with 1-16 I/O threads; memtier runs on cores 16-31. Pipelining is 1/10/25/50, over a local UNIX socket with persistence off, on AWS c8g.8xlarge (32-core ARM64). Each point is the median of 31 runs, with a warmup SET pass excluded.
claimed_speedup: cache-benchmarks results/output.json (median of 31 runs, pipeline 1, 8 server threads): Pogocache 1.2.0 GET 3,080,753 ops/s vs Redis 8.2.1 1,513,408 (~2.0x) and memcached 1.6.38 2,601,307 (~1.18x); SET 2,948,581 vs Redis 1,669,915 (~1.8x) and memcached 1,271,805 (~2.3x) (ratios derived from page data). GET p99 is 0.119 ms vs Redis 0.207 ms and memcached 0.191 ms. CPU cycles/op are ~7,053 vs Redis ~9,957 and memcached ~13,400 (derived from page data: perf cycles / total ops). Pogocache beats both Redis and memcached on SET and GET at every thread count (1-16) and pipeline depth (1/10/25/50) in the suite. The figures 3,145,960 vs Redis 909,837 (~3.5x), 111us and 6968 cycles come from the hidden table in the Pogocache README. That table records the older July 2025 run (Pogocache v0.0.1, Redis 8.0.2; cache-benchmarks commit adc83b4) and is overstated against current results.
hardware: AWS c8g.8xlarge, 32-core non-NUMA ARM64
tradeoffs: Newer/less battle-tested than Redis/Memcached in production; supports Memcache, RESP and Postgres wire protocols but not full Redis command set (data structures, scripting, etc.)
caveats: The suite is written and run by Pogocache's author (tidwall), so it is not independent. No compiler or build flags are stated for any server; only versions and commits are given. The headline table in the Pogocache README (~3.5x Redis) is stale: it comes from a July 2025 run with Redis 8.0.2. The current suite with Redis 8.2.1 shows ~2x on GET at 8 threads. The README claim 'faster than Garnet' holds only at low pipelining: at pipeline 25/50 Garnet beats Pogocache by a wide margin (e.g. 8 threads, pipeline 50: Garnet GET 29.5M vs Pogocache 11.4M ops/s). The cache-benchmarks repo has no license file.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/tidwall/pogocache; README table pointing to linked cache-benchmarks repo, opened directly

verification.tier_reason: tidwall/cache-benchmarks publishes its benchmark code (bench-all.sh, cmd/bench/main.go) and raw results (results/output.json), with the hardware (AWS c8g.8xlarge) and server versions stated. It lists no compiler or build flags, and Pogocache's own author wrote and ran it, so it is first-party with partial methodology (C, not B).
verification.notes: The claim is sound against the baselines: Pogocache beats Redis and memcached at every configuration in the suite. However, the record's numbers are the stale README figures, now replaced by the current output.json medians. The tier drops from B to C because the only benchmark is author-run and has no compiler or flags. Metadata checks out: MIT, 2,518 stars, last commit 2026-08-05, active, not a fork.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: throughput ranking (pipeline 1, 8 threads): pogocache 3,145,960 ops/s vs memcache 2,601,306, garnet 1,548,050, dragonfly 1,407,584, valkey 1,331,683, redis 909,837 (~3.5x Redis, ~1.2x Memcached); lowest latency (111us) and fewest CPU cycles/op (6968) of the group
corrected_fields.workload: memtier_benchmark 100K SET + 100K GET ops per client, 256 clients over 16 I/O threads, pipelining 1/10/25/50, on AWS c8g.8xlarge (32-core ARM64), Unix socket, persistence off, 31 runs per point (median reported)
corrected_fields.caveats: The cache-benchmarks suite comparing pogocache to Redis/Valkey/Dragonfly/Garnet/Memcache is written and run by pogocache's own author (tidwall), so it is not a fully independent third party, even though the methodology (31 runs, median, stated hardware, stated versions) is unusually rigorous; exact compiler/build flags for each server are not listed, only released versions/commits

name: RobinHood (tail-latency-aware cache repartitioning)
baseline: OneRFpolicy: a single shared off-the-shelf memcached cache per application server, matching Microsoft OneRF's production configuration. Also compared: TAO++ (static per-backend allocation) and emulated LAMA++, Cliffhanger++ and FAIR++.
workload: Testbed of 16 application servers and 34 backend servers across 50 Azure VMs. The servers host 20 backend services (KV store, MySQL cluster, matrix-multiply recommender) modeled on OneRF's 20 most-queried backends. Each application server has a local 32GB memcached. Traffic comes from OneRF production statistics, averaging ~200k queries/s (500k peak), with injected backend load and latency spikes. The metric is the fraction of time a 150ms P99 request-latency SLO is met.
claimed_speedup: Under backend load spikes on the OneRF-modeled testbed, RobinHood meets a 150ms P99 request-latency goal 99.7% of the time, whereas the next best policy meets it only 70% of the time. Sec. 5.2 names the next best policy as OneRFpolicy, a single shared memcached cache matching Microsoft OneRF's production setup: it violates the 150ms P99 SLO 30% of the time vs <0.3% for RobinHood.
hardware: 50 Microsoft Azure D16 v3 VMs: 2.4 GHz Intel E5-2673v3 (8 cores), 64GB memory, 400GB SSD, 8Gbit/s network
tradeoffs: Optimizes cross-backend cache-space allocation, not the per-cache eviction policy itself; requires a central resource-allocation (RBC) controller polling all backend caches, adding a coordination layer on top of plain memcached; reallocation decisions are rate-limited to avoid thrashing (ignores reallocations faster than 5s)
caveats: The metric is SLO attainment (share of time meeting a 150ms P99), not a throughput or speed ratio. The next-best baseline is a caching policy (one shared memcached cache without partitioning), not a slower memcached. RobinHood repartitions off-the-shelf memcached, so it is a cache resource-allocation system, not a new eviction algorithm. The testbed is Go plus a Python controller, last touched in 2019. No compiler or flags are stated.
found_via: gh api repos/dasebe/robinhoodcache/readme; OSDI'18 paper PDF (usenix.org)

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed OSDI'18 paper. It states the 99.7% vs 70% result for meeting a 150ms P99 goal (abstract, Fig. 3) and compares against two production policies (OneRFpolicy, which is a single shared off-the-shelf memcached cache, and TAO++) plus emulated LAMA, Cliffhanger and FAIR. The testbed code is public in the repo and the CPU is given (Azure D16 v3, E5-2673v3), but no compiler or flags are stated, so it is not A.
verification.notes: All metadata matched gh (BSD-3-Clause, 95 stars, last commit 2019-07-08, not archived, not a fork). The main fix is that the 70% 'next best' policy is OneRFpolicy (single shared cache), not a static-partitioning policy. Static partitioning is TAO++.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: RobinHood meets a 150ms P99 latency goal 99.7% of the time during load spikes, versus only 70% of the time for the next-best static cache-partitioning policy tested
corrected_fields.baseline: memcached-style per-backend caching without dynamic repartitioning
corrected_fields.hardware: Servers provisioned with 2.4GHz Intel Xeon E5-2673v3
corrected_fields.workload: 50-server production-trace testbed emulating a large web service (20 backend systems, memcached-compatible per-backend caches) under load spikes, measuring P99 request latency against a 150ms SLO
corrected_fields.caveats: Baseline is 'next best' static/off-the-shelf cache partitioning across memcached-like backends, not literally raw memcached itself, so baseline_in_list is false and confidence is reduced accordingly; this is a cache resource-allocation system rather than a new eviction algorithm

name: S3-FIFO
baseline: LRU (Meta CacheLib's optimized LRU; also CacheLib's optimized 2Q and TinyLFU, plus Segcache)
workload: Throughput: an S3-FIFO prototype in Meta CacheLib replays only a synthetic Zipf (alpha=1.0) trace. The trace is 100*n million requests over n million 4KB objects (n = thread count), run at 1-16 threads with a large cache (LRU miss ratio 0.02) and a small one (0.21). Miss ratio: libCacheSim simulation over 6594 production traces from 14 datasets (MSR, FIU, CloudPhysics, CDN1/2, Tencent, Wikimedia, Alibaba, Twitter, Meta KV/CDN, ...).
claimed_speedup: S3-FIFO achieves more than 6x higher throughput than the highly-optimized LRU in Meta's CacheLib with 16 threads, at both small and large cache sizes (synthetic Zipf trace). The throughput gap is larger still vs CacheLib's optimized 2Q and TinyLFU. Separately, in libCacheSim simulation over 6594 traces from 14 datasets, S3-FIFO has lower miss ratios than state-of-the-art algorithms and the lowest mean miss ratio on 10 of the 14 datasets.
compiler_and_flags: Artifact build script (Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23 mybench/build.sh) uses CMake build type RelWithDebInfo with Ninja; compiler not named
hardware: CloudLab Clemson c6420 nodes for the prototype (the paper does not name the CPU model). Turbo boost off, one thread pinned per core, all memory allocated on the same NUMA node with numactl.
stars_or_usage: 347 stars (1a1a11a/libCacheSim, simulator home of S3FIFO.c); artifact repo Thesys-lab/sosp23-s3fifo 145 stars; CacheLib prototype in Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23
tradeoffs: Uses three FIFO queues (small, main, ghost) instead of one list; ghost-queue metadata adds memory overhead; small-queue size ratio (S) needs tuning per workload
caveats: The throughput numbers come from a single synthetic Zipf(1.0) workload in a modified CacheLib, not from production traces. The miss-ratio results come from simulation. The paper names no CPU model (only CloudLab c6420 nodes) and no compiler, so this stays at tier B. The S3-FIFO simulator code is in libCacheSim (libCacheSim/cache/eviction/S3FIFO.c). The throughput prototype is in a separate CacheLib fork snapshot (Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23, Apache-2.0).
found_via: gh search repos 'S3-FIFO cache'; junchengyang.com publication page; arXiv search 'S3-FIFO cache eviction'

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed SOSP'23 paper. It states S3-FIFO in CacheLib reaches >6x the throughput of CacheLib's optimized LRU at 16 threads, with a larger gap vs 2Q and TinyLFU (Sec. 1, Sec. 5.3, Fig. 8). The prototype benchmark code is public (Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23 mybench/, CMake RelWithDebInfo), but the paper names only CloudLab c6420 nodes, not a CPU model or compiler, so it is not A.
verification.notes: The record's '1559 evaluated traces' does not appear in the paper, which says 6594 traces from 14 datasets. The record also said the throughput test replayed CDN/Twitter/Meta traces, but the paper says it used only a synthetic Zipf trace. Both are fixed. gh metadata matches the record: Apache-2.0, 347 stars, last commit 2026-09-26, active (GitHub lists the repo language as C++, while S3FIFO.c is C).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: S3-FIFO achieves more than 6x higher throughput than the highly-optimized LRU implementation in Meta's CacheLib at 16 cores; the gap widens further versus 2Q and TinyLFU; also reduces FIFO's miss ratio across most of the 1559 evaluated traces (see the paper's Fig.6-7 percentile plots)
corrected_fields.workload: CacheLib-based KV-cache prototype replaying synthetic Zipf and production CDN/KV traces (CDN1, CDN2, Twitter, Meta), throughput scaling measured across 1-16 cores
corrected_fields.hardware: CloudLab testbed nodes; the paper cites an AMD EPYC 9654P only as an example of a modern many-core CPU, not confirmed in the extracted text as the exact throughput-test machine
corrected_fields.stars_or_usage: 347 stars (libCacheSim); implemented inside Meta's CacheLib per the paper
corrected_fields.caveats: Exact CPU model for the throughput experiment and compiler/flags are not pinned down in the text we could extract, so capped at tier B not A

name: SIEVE
workload: 1559 traces from 7 datasets (247,017 million requests, 14,852 million objects; Twitter, Meta, Wikimedia, TencentPhoto and two proprietary CDNs) replayed in libCacheSim for miss ratio. Separately, a Cachelib (C++) prototype replays two production KV traces (Meta, Twitter) with 1-16 threads, with cache size 4 x nthreads GB, to measure throughput.
claimed_speedup: Cachelib-based prototype: SIEVE is 16% faster than Cachelib's optimized LRU (17% vs TwoQ) at 1 thread on both the Meta and Twitter KV traces. At 16 threads it has more than 2x the throughput of optimized LRU and TwoQ on the Meta trace (the contributions list says 125% higher than optimized LRU). Optimized LRU itself scales about 6x from 1 to 16 threads on Twitter; only the unoptimized LRU plateaus at 4 threads. Miss ratio in libCacheSim: on CDN1 at the large cache size, SIEVE reduces FIFO's miss ratio by a mean of 21%, and by more than 42% on 10% of traces (p90 whisker). Over 1559 traces it reduces ARC's miss ratio by up to 63.2% (mean 1.5%). The paper frames that 1.5% mean as significant next to ARC's own mean 6.3% reduction over LRU; the 1.5% is smaller than the 6.3%, not larger.
hardware: Dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6142 @ 2.6GHz, 384GB DDR4 DRAM (CloudLab c6420 node), turbo boost off, threads pinned within one NUMA node
stars_or_usage: 347 stars (libCacheSim); sievecache.com (redirects to cachemon.github.io/SIEVE-website) lists adopters including Immudb, TiDB, Pelikan, DragonFly, DNSCrypt-proxy, PostgREST and Ceph
tradeoffs: Needs a per-object 'visited' bit like CLOCK; underperforms TwoQ/LHD/ARC at very small cache sizes because new objects can't demonstrate popularity before being evicted
caveats: The paper states the CPU model, NUMA pinning and turbo-boost setting for the throughput prototype but not the compiler or optimization flags, so it is capped at tier B. The miss-ratio numbers come from the libCacheSim simulator. The throughput numbers come from a separate Cachelib-based C++ prototype (Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23), not from libCacheSim. The >2x throughput result at 16 threads is reported for the Meta trace only. The paper is internally inconsistent about ARC's mean reduction over LRU: the introduction says 6.7% (up to 33.7%) and Section 4.2 says 6.3%. libCacheSim's Sieve.c is a simulator policy, not a drop-in production cache.
found_via: arXiv/DBLP search for 'SIEVE cache eviction'; junchengyang.com publication page; gh search repos 'SIEVE cache eviction'

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NSDI'24 paper compares SIEVE against LRU (Cachelib's optimized LRU for throughput) plus FIFO, ARC and 7 other policies for miss ratio. The code is public (cacheMon/NSDI24-SIEVE simulator snapshot; Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23 prototype) and the CPU model is stated (c6420, Intel Gold 6142 @ 2.6 GHz, turbo off, one NUMA node), but the compiler and flags are not, so it cannot be A.
verification.notes: The original claim misattributed the 4-thread plateau to the optimized LRU; in the paper it applies only to the unoptimized LRU. The claim also inverted the 1.5% vs 6.3% comparison. The core >2x-at-16-threads and 63.2%-vs-ARC numbers are on the page. The metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 347 stars, not archived or a fork, last commit 2026-09-26 (active). The phrase 'production-ready' does not appear on sievecache.com; the site lists adopters, so stars_or_usage was reworded.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Prototype throughput is >2x an optimized 16-thread LRU (LRU plateaus at 4 threads while SIEVE keeps scaling); reduces mean miss ratio vs FIFO by 21% (up to 42% at p90) on CDN1 at large cache size, and vs ARC by up to 63.2% (mean 1.5%, itself more than the 6.3% mean reduction ARC gets over LRU)
corrected_fields.workload: 1559 CDN/KV traces (247B requests, Twitter/Meta/Wikimedia/proprietary CDN) replayed in libCacheSim for miss-ratio, plus a multi-threaded prototype cache replaying KV-cache workloads for throughput scaling from 1-16 threads
corrected_fields.stars_or_usage: 347 stars (libCacheSim, the reference implementation); promoted as production-ready on sievecache.com
corrected_fields.caveats: Paper states CPU model, NUMA pinning and turbo-boost setting for the throughput prototype but not the compiler or optimization flags, so capped at tier B; miss-ratio numbers come from libCacheSim simulation while the throughput numbers come from a separate hand-built prototype

name: Cachelot
workload: A Python script (test/memory_consumption.py) generates 2GB of random keys (10-60 chars) and values in four size ranges: 10B-1KB, 1-4KB, 4KB-1MB, and 10B-1MB. It fills cachelotd and Memcached, each limited to 2GB, over 10 shuffled runs and measures 'effective memory', the total bytes of surviving keys and values.
claimed_speedup: The page says Cachelot 'keeps more items in the same amount of RAM than Memcached (saves up to 15% RAM, depending on the data and store patterns)', with 5-7% metadata overhead. The chart data (benchmarks.js, 2048MB budget, 10 runs) shows effective memory of 91.2-93.9% vs 79.5% for Memcached on small values (10B-1KB), 94.2-98.6% vs 86.7% on 1-4KB, 93.3-96.9% vs 87.2-87.3% on 4KB-1MB, and 93.4-97.4% vs 86.9-87.0% on mixed. That is up to about 14.4 points of the budget, or 7-18% more stored data (derived from page data). The README says Cachelot 'is faster in terms of latency' but gives no numbers.
tradeoffs: Single-threaded server design (scales via sharding/multiple processes, not one multithreaded process); fixed pre-allocated memory pool; only a subset of the memcached wire protocol
caveats: No CPU model, compiler, flags or Memcached version are stated for the vs-Memcached test. It measures memory efficiency only; the latency claim has no numbers, and a memslap throughput script (src/benchmark/memslap_benchmark.sh) exists with no published results. The current script's MEMORY_LIMIT is 4GB while the page reports 2GB runs. There is no independent verification. The last commit on master was 2023-04-12 (pushed_at 2024-08-07 is not a commit), over 3 years ago.

name: Dragonfly
workload: memtier_benchmark SET/GET ops (-d 256) against Redis on m5.large/m5.xlarge, and against Memcached on c6gn.16xlarge; also idle/peak memory usage during BGSAVE-equivalent snapshot
claimed_speedup: Vendor README: on c6gn.16xlarge, 25x the throughput of a single single-threaded Redis process, crossing 3.8M QPS. Vs Memcached on c6gn.16xlarge: SET 3,844K vs 806K QPS (~4.8x) and GET 3,717K vs 2,100K QPS (~1.8x) (ratios derived from page data); Memcached had the lower GET p99 (0.34 ms vs 1 ms). Vs Redis on m5.large: about parity (SET 173K vs 159K; GET 191K vs 194K). Vs Redis on m5.xlarge: SET 279K vs 190K, GET 305K vs 220K. Memory: ~30% lower idle memory than Redis, and Redis peak during BGSAVE was almost 3x Dragonfly's. The 25x is contested. Redis's June 2022 rebuttal ran a 40-shard Redis 7.0 Cluster on the same c6gn.16xlarge and reported 18-40% MORE throughput than Dragonfly (e.g. GET pipeline 1: 4.43M vs 3.8M reproduced). The third-party tidwall/cache-benchmarks (c8g.8xlarge; Dragonfly 1.30.3 vs Redis 8.2.1 with io-threads) shows mixed results. Redis is faster at 8 server threads (GET 1.51M vs 1.41M), and Dragonfly is ~2.2x faster at 16 threads (GET 2.94M vs 1.32M). Memcached beats Dragonfly on GET at every thread count and pipeline depth.
hardware: AWS m5.large, m5.xlarge, c6gn.16xlarge, r6g/c7g (instance types stated; CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Business Source License restricts running it as a competing hosted service (converts to Apache-2.0 on 2030-11-01); single shared-nothing multi-threaded architecture differs operationally from Redis single-thread model
caveats: The 25x headline is a vendor claim against one single-threaded Redis process on a 64-vCPU instance, which is not how Redis is scaled. Redis's own 2022 test on the same c6gn.16xlarge with a 40-shard Redis 7.0 Cluster measured 18-40% higher throughput than Dragonfly. That test is also vendor-run and dates from 2022, against Dragonfly built on 2022-06-03. The README states no CPU model, compiler, flags or baseline versions, and publishes no benchmark code. The earlier caveat that tidwall/cache-benchmarks 'corroborates Dragonfly beating Redis/Memcached' is wrong. In that suite Dragonfly beats Redis 8.2.1 (io-threads) only at higher thread counts, loses to it at 8 server threads, and loses to memcached on GET in every configuration; that suite's author also makes the competing Pogocache. License is BUSL-1.1 (not OSI; Apache-2.0 on the Change Date of 2030-11-01, and production use is restricted for competing in-memory data store services).

name: IKV (Inlined Key-Value Store)
workload: Custom Java multithreaded client (inlinedio/ikv-java-client benchmarks; JedisCluster for Redis) issuing blocking single-field GETs at fixed loads (25K/50K/100K/1M/3M QPS). It used 16 threads, 1M docs (~15 B keys, 3x50 B fields) and a 30 s window, against IKV embedded in the client process and a 16-shard ElastiCache Redis 7.1 cluster in the same AZ. A second test used tiered storage with Zipfian keys, 6000 B values and 16 IKV threads, against a 1-thread, 1-shard ElastiCache Redis.
claimed_speedup: In-memory GET with 16 client threads over 1M docs (150 B values), at 100K QPS: IKV avg 3.13 us / p50 2.89 / p99 5.65 vs a 16-shard AWS ElastiCache Redis 7.1 cluster at avg 319 us / p50 305 / p99 514 (~100x lower latency, derived from page data). IKV also held 1M and 3M QPS, which Redis could not reach from the single client. In the tiered test (1:4 memory:data, Zipfian), IKV averaged 118.25 us vs 225.06 us for in-memory 1-shard Redis (~1.9x, derived from page data), but IKV's p99 was worse (747.65 us vs 348.88 us). The ~100x gap is mostly the network round trip that embedding removes (an in-process lookup vs a remote ElastiCache call over TCP), not a faster storage engine.
hardware: In-memory test: client and embedded IKV on AWS c5.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 32 GiB). Redis was AWS ElastiCache Redis 7.1 with 16 shards (1 primary, 0 replicas each) on cache.r5.xlarge nodes in the same AZ (us-west-2a). Tiered test: client on c5d.4xlarge (400 GiB local SSD) vs 1-shard ElastiCache cache.r6g.xlarge / cache.r6gd.xlarge. CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: IKV is an embedded/in-process library colocated with the application (no network hop) rather than a shared remote cache, so much of the 100x gap is network round-trip elimination rather than a faster core engine; eventual consistency instead of Redis's stronger read-after-write guarantees; requires a separate data-plane (streams/object storage) to keep embedded replicas in sync
caveats: The full report (Google Doc, readable through its txt export) gives instance types but no CPU model, compiler or flags. The comparison is embedded (in-process, no network) vs networked (remote ElastiCache over TCP through the Jedis client). That makes it a valid deployment-architecture comparison for read-heavy, eventually consistent ML feature serving, but not a like-for-like engine comparison. Most of Redis's ~300 us is network round trip plus client overhead. A fair engine test would use Redis over localhost or a Unix socket, or another embedded KV. The tiered '2x faster than Redis' holds for average latency only: p99 is worse for IKV (747.65 vs 348.88 us). The tiered test used 16 IKV threads vs 1 Redis thread, and the report's text and table disagree on thread counts. A single client machine drove the load. The repo is stale (last commit 2024-05-14).

verification.notes: Judgment on the embedded-vs-networked comparison: it is a legitimate real-use-case latency win, but '100x faster than Redis' mostly measures removing the network hop, not IKV's engine against Redis's engine. The claim is overstated as a library-speed claim. Tier stays C. I was able to read the Google Doc report, which fills in hardware and methodology. name: W-TinyLFU (C++ header-only, based on the TinyLFU paper)
workload: Synthetic Zipf(0.7/0.94) and SPC1-like traces plus real YouTube/Wikipedia/DS1/S3/OLTP traces evaluated for hit ratio, comparing TinyLFU-admission-augmented LRU/Random/LFU against plain LRU, ARC, SLRU, LRU-K and others (algorithm's own paper; this specific repo is an independent C++11 header-only reimplementation)
claimed_speedup: Per the paper (not this port), W-TinyLFU with a 1% window matched or beat every other evaluated policy on the majority of traces, including LRU, ARC and LIRS. It outperformed all other policies on DS1, SPC1-like and the search-engine traces. On OLTP, F1 and F2, the 1% window was not the top performer; a 20-40% window was needed. On P8/P12 it led at all but the largest cache sizes. The ~89% figure is TinyLFU's memory saving over a strawman sliding-window sketch (Zipf 0.9, 1K cache, 9K histogram), not a result against LRU.
tradeoffs: This specific repo explicitly omits thread-safety and hash-collision protection ('barebones' header-only port); the underlying TinyLFU paper's hit-ratio numbers come from a Java prototype and from Caffeine, not from this C++ port directly
caveats: The quantitative hit-ratio results come from the original paper's Java simulator and Caffeine evaluation. They were not re-measured on this C++11 header-only port, so the entry is tier C even though the algorithm's paper is well cited. The README says thread-safety and hash-collision protection are absent. The repo has no LICENSE file. Caffeine itself (the canonical TinyLFU implementation) is already catalogued and excluded.

name: ALP (Adaptive Lossless Floating-Point Compression)
baseline: Zstd, Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, Patas (existing lightweight and general-purpose floating-point compressors)
workload: Single/multi-threaded (1/8/16 thread) SCAN and SUM queries over compressed double/float columns from real-world datasets (food_prices, city_temperature, bitcoin_transactions, gov26, nyc29), plus separate compression-ratio benchmarks over the Public BI float/double corpus.
claimed_speedup: SIGMOD'24 paper Table 5 (Ice Lake micro-benchmark, tuples per cycle, averaged over all datasets): ALP compresses 14x faster than Zstd, 9x faster than Gorilla, 12x faster than Chimp and Chimp128, 8x faster than Patas, 47x faster than Elf and 251x faster than PDE. It decompresses 26x faster than Zstd, 55x than Gorilla, 66x than Chimp, 65x than Chimp128, 17x than Patas, 215x than Elf and 7x than PDE. Figure 1: '1-2 orders of magnitude faster in [de]compression than all competing schemes'. End-to-end in Tectorwise (Table 6, Figure 6): SCAN and SUM on ALP beat every other scheme and even uncompressed data. City-Temp compression is 4x faster than Patas and 7x faster than Gorilla, and Zstd is 11x slower. Compression ratio (Table 4): ALP averages 21.7 bits/value against Zstd's 20.6, so Zstd is slightly better on average; ALP beats all the other schemes.
compiler_and_flags: clang++ (the root CMakeLists allows only Clang; toolchain/i4i_4xlarge.cmake uses /usr/bin/clang++; version not stated). -O3 per the paper. bench_end_to_end CMake adds -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -mavx512dq. Scalar variant: -O3 -fno-slp-vectorize -fno-vectorize. g++ is used only to build the PDE baseline.
hardware: Main results (Figure 1, Table 5, end-to-end Figure 6 and Table 6) on Intel Ice Lake Xeon 8375C at 3.5 GHz (AWS i4i.4xlarge; the end-to-end run used 16 cores / 32 SMT and 256 GB RAM). Decompression was also run on AMD EPYC 7R13 (Zen3), Apple M1, AWS Graviton2 (Neoverse-N1) and Graviton3 (Paper Table 3).
stars_or_usage: 234 stars; integrated into DuckDB, KuzuDB, and liquid-cache
tradeoffs: Targets IEEE754 float/double columns specifically, not general-purpose compression; decimal-heavy data benefits most, high-entropy/high-precision random values compress less well and fall back to a dictionary+FoR split scheme.
caveats: The headline numbers are the authors' own (SIGMOD 2024), backed by the SIGMOD ARI package with all three badges (including Results Reproduced) and the SIGMOD Best Artifact Award. The paper is openly available at ir.cwi.nl/pub/33334/33334.pdf and bronze-OA at ACM. Zstd matches or slightly beats ALP's compression ratio on average (20.6 vs 21.7 bits/value); ALP only wins on ratio when cascaded with other lightweight encodings. The ARI report says the Figure 6 plotting script is missing. The repo CSV publication/end_to_end_bench/result holds raw cycle counts, not ratios.
found_via: Linked from the FastLanes README publications list; repo's availability_reproducibility_initiative_report.md

verification.tier_reason: The SIGMOD 2024 paper (open copy at ir.cwi.nl) compares ALP with Zstd, Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, Patas, PDE and Elf. It names the CPU model (Intel Xeon 8375C Ice Lake, Table 3) and the -O3 flags, and the repo sets the compiler (toolchain/i4i_4xlarge.cmake uses clang++, and CMake allows only Clang). The benchmark code is public: publication/source_code/bench_speed, bench_end_to_end (-O3 -march=native -mavx512dq) and bench_compression_ratio, run by publication/script/master_script.sh. That meets tier A.
verification.notes: The record's claim that the paper is paywalled with no preprint is wrong: the CWI repository hosts the full PDF, and I read it. I kept tier A. I replaced the vague claimed_speedup with the Table 5 multipliers and softened the compression-ratio claim against Zstd. The raw end-to-end CSV agrees with the paper: summed cycles show SCAN on ALP about 18-20x cheaper than on Zstd with one thread (derived from page data).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: ALP is reported superior in decoding speed, compression ratio, and compression speed across every tested scheme (Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, Patas, Zstd, uncompressed, PDE) per the paper's results and the repo's benchmark CSVs; exact multipliers are in the repo's publication/end_to_end_bench results
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: Clang++/g++ via CMake (>=3.22); exact build steps and flags documented in BENCHMARKING.md and run by publication/script/master_script.sh
corrected_fields.hardware: Multiple documented target platforms in the reproducibility package: Intel Ice Lake (AVX512, e.g. AWS i4i.4xlarge), AMD Zen 3 (AVX2, AWS M6a/C6a), Apple M1, AWS Graviton 2/3 (NEON)

Tier A is justified instead by the repo's ACM SIGMOD Availability & Reproducibility Initiative package (all three badges, including 'Results Reproduced'), which documents hardware, dependencies, and build/run steps end to end, and by the benchmark CSVs present in the repo.

name: Bodo DataFrames
language: Python (JIT-compiled to native code via an MPI-based C++ runtime)
workload: NYC Taxi FHVHV 'monthly trips with precipitation': the 1,036,465,968-row / 24-column Parquet dataset (24.7 GiB, read from S3) is joined with the 5,538-row Central Park weather CSV. A per-row Python UDF assigns hour-of-day buckets, then the job groups by count and mean trip_miles, sorts, and writes Parquet. The README says 'average trip duration', but the code aggregates trip distance. Single-node run on one AWS r6i.16xlarge (32 physical cores, 512 GiB RAM).
claimed_speedup: Measured with the Bodo JIT path (run_bodo.py --use_jit), not the Bodo DataFrames pandas API. Single r6i.16xlarge (Mar 2025): Bodo 27.71s vs Polars 282.34s (~10.2x) and vs Daft 69.59s (~2.5x). 4x r6i.16xlarge (Dec 2024): Bodo 17s vs PySpark 389s, Dask 915s and Modin+Ray 4155s; the chart labels these 20x / 50x / 250x, while the README text says '20-240x'. 4 nodes vs Daft (Mar 2025): 17.54s vs 37.78s (~2x). The same README's laptop-scale table shows the Bodo DataFrames API slower than Polars: 5.63s vs 1.244s, and 10.221s vs 4.744s on ~20M rows (derived from page data).
hardware: AWS EC2 r6i.16xlarge (32 physical cores, 512 GiB RAM); cluster variant uses 4x r6i.16xlarge
tradeoffs: Drop-in pandas-API replacement but relies on JIT compilation and MPI for parallelism; the Bodo Platform build used for the cluster run links a forked version of Arrow for faster Parquet reads (bodo-ai/arrow-cpp-feedstock), a deviation from stock Apache Arrow
caveats: First-party benchmark (Bodo's own repo), not an independent suite, and numbers are read from bar-chart PNGs rather than a raw results table. The charts measure the Bodo JIT path: the main README carries a 'TODO: updated graph with Taxi benchmark including Bodo DataFrames Pandas API', and the benchmark README's laptop table shows the Bodo DataFrames API slower than Polars (5.63s vs 1.244s; 10.221s vs 4.744s). The Polars implementation buckets hours with map_elements and a Python UDF (row-by-row Python over ~1B rows), which Bodo JIT compiles to native code, so the ~10x single-node gap largely reflects a non-idiomatic Polars baseline. Bodo ran on the Bodo Platform with a forked Arrow for faster Parquet reads. The package table lists bodo 2025.8.2 while the charts date from Dec 2024 / Mar 2025. No compiler/flags are given, and the CPU is identified only by instance type. The single-node comparison excludes pandas.

name: BtrBlocks
baseline: Apache Parquet (generated/read via the Apache Arrow C++ library) and Apache ORC
workload: In-memory decompression throughput and S3 cold-column-scan dollar-cost, measured on the 5 largest Public BI Benchmark datasets (~2451 columns) and all 22 TPC-H queries.
claimed_speedup: Public BI in-memory decompression: 2.6x, 3.6x and 3.8x faster than Parquet, Parquet+Snappy and Parquet+Zstd on average. TPC-H in-memory: 2.6x, 3.9x and 4.2x faster. S3 column scans on Public BI are 9x cheaper than compressed Parquet variants and 20x cheaper than uncompressed Parquet on average. Over all 22 TPC-H queries, Parquet, Parquet+Snappy and Parquet+Zstd cost 5.5x, 3.6x and 2.8x more than BtrBlocks.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 10.3.1 on Amazon Linux 2, kernel 5.10 (paper). The paper states no optimization flags; the repo CMakeLists adds -march=native -g on top of the CMake build-type defaults.
hardware: AWS c5n.18xlarge: Intel Xeon Platinum 8000 series (Skylake-SP), 36 x 3.5 GHz cores (72 threads, hyperthreading disabled for benchmarks), AVX2/AVX512, 192 GiB RAM, 100 Gbit networking
tradeoffs: README states it 'currently requires an x86 platform' and is only built/tested on Linux and macOS; test suite described as 'rudimentary'; no true random-access-by-row API (would require reimplementation, per a later independent evaluation).
caveats: These are the SIGMOD 2023 authors' own measurements. The Parquet/ORC comparison harness and exact build flags are not published; the repo's engine-comparison directory says it was removed because of DeWitt clauses. A later VLDB 2025 paper by competing FastLanes authors (not independent) re-ran BtrBlocks on an AWS i4i.4xlarge. It found BtrBlocks decoded about 7x slower than FastLanes (encoding was 1.37x slower, derived from that paper's Table 4). BtrBlocks gained nothing from AVX512 and could not do single-value random access without an API reimplementation. name: FastLanes
baseline: Apache Parquet (Snappy and Zstd variants, written and read with DuckDB v1.2's Parquet implementation) and DuckDB v1.2's native storage format; also BtrBlocks
workload: Decoding/encoding throughput (rowgroups/sec) across real-world datasets and a single-value random-access latency micro-benchmark, comparing the FastLanes file format against DuckDB, Parquet+Snappy, Parquet+Zstd, and BtrBlocks.
claimed_speedup: Decoding (Table 4, i4i.4xlarge Ice Lake): on average 29x faster than DuckDB's native format, 43x faster than Parquet+Snappy, 44x faster than Parquet+Zstd and 7x faster than BtrBlocks. Totals: 16.32 ms vs 483.45, 712.55, 731.45 and 115.43 ms. Encoding is not faster: FastLanes v0.1 took 81,341.63 ms against 5,867.07 (Parquet+Snappy), 6,927.52 (Parquet+Zstd) and 20,347.82 (DuckDB). That makes it about 14x, 12x and 4x slower, and only about 1.4x faster than BtrBlocks (111,091.39 ms) (derived from page data). Random access (Table 5; text says 315x/416x/800x/5x): first-value retrieval takes 0.14 ms, 315.62x faster than Parquet+Snappy, 413.66x than Parquet+Zstd, 813.57x than BtrBlocks and 5.96x than DuckDB.
compiler_and_flags: The paper does not name the compiler (the artifact README lists 'gcc / clang'; the current FastLanes CMakeLists defaults to clang++ on non-Windows). FastLanes is built as a CMake Release. The SIMD micro-benchmark (Table 6) used -O3, -O3 -mavx2 and -O3 -mavx512dq.
hardware: All experiments on AWS EC2 i4i.4xlarge: Intel Xeon (Ice Lake), 16 vCPUs, 128 GiB RAM (paper Sec. 4; no CPU model number given). Only the expression-pool micro-benchmark (Table 7, footnote 4) ran on an Apple MacBook Pro M4.
tradeoffs: Encoding (compression) speed in the v0.1 code path is explicitly unoptimized per the paper; the file format only recently reached format-stability (v0.36+), so tooling/ecosystem support lags far behind Parquet; zero external dependencies but currently no true random-access-by-row-position support (block decode still required).
caveats: These are the authors' own VLDB 2025 numbers (Afroozeh & Boncz, CWI). The artifact repo cwida/fastlanes-vldb2025 reproduces them. Parquet was run through DuckDB v1.2's Parquet reader and writer, not parquet-cpp/Arrow. The headline multipliers are decoding-only: FastLanes v0.1 encoding is 4-14x slower than DuckDB and Parquet and beats only BtrBlocks, which the authors attribute to an unoptimized encoder. Random access was simulated with LIMIT 1 queries on Parquet and DuckDB and with full block decoding for BtrBlocks. The table and text multipliers differ slightly (413.66x vs 416x, 813.57x vs 800x).
found_via: arXiv/DBLP search for cwida FastLanes VLDB papers; PDF opened directly at vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p4629-afroozeh.pdf

verification.tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed VLDB 2025 paper, and its public artifact repo (cwida/fastlanes-vldb2025: master_script.py, scripts/, plus FastLanes CMake targets benchmark_decompression_time and benchmark_random_access) reproduces Tables 3-6 against Parquet, DuckDB and BtrBlocks. verification.notes: The record's '29x faster decoding/encoding' is overstated: the Table 4 multipliers are for decoding, and FastLanes encoding is slower than Parquet and DuckDB. The record also put Table 5 on the M4, but the M4 footnote belongs to the Table 7 expression-pool experiment. Metadata is confirmed: MIT, 713 stars, last commit 2026-04-22 (active, dev branch).

name: Velox
baseline: Presto Java execution engine (stock Presto vs Prestissimo, i.e. Presto with Velox C++ workers)
workload: TPC-H at 3TB (ORC, no zstd compression, lineitem/orders co-partitioned), hand-written query formulations, selected queries Q1, Q6 (CPU-bound) and Q13, Q19 (shuffle/IO-heavy), warm local cache; plus a replay of Meta production interactive-analytics traffic on two clusters with identical hardware

Replay of production interactive-analytics traffic on two identical clusters: average speedup about 6-7x, with many queries above 10x. Prestissimo also served the same shadowed production workload with 3x fewer servers.
hardware: 80-node cluster, each node with 64GB RAM and 2x2TB SSD; CPU model not stated in the paper
tradeoffs: Velox itself is only a C++ execution-engine library with no SQL parser/optimizer/catalog; this result actually benchmarks facebookincubator/axiom (a thin SQL layer built on Velox); must be built from source (no release binaries), which is memory- and time-intensive

Velox wins only 4 of 43 queries (0-based numbering): Q32 10.67s vs 24.23s (2.27x), Q18 12.18s vs 21.84s (1.79x), Q33 10.49s vs 17.57s (1.67x) and Q34 11.13s vs 17.06s (1.53x). It is more than 100x slower on Q0, Q1 and Q19. Against the same-format entry, ClickHouse (Parquet, single) on 2026-09-26, the totals are 214.09s vs 123.75s: Velox wins 5 of 43 queries by 1.08-1.95x, loses 37, and is about 100x slower on Q29 (18.85s vs 0.187s). All of these figures are derived from page data. The 'dishonest academic paper' remark is in ClickBench's velox/README.md, not the top-level README. The paper's numbers are first-party Meta results for a distributed Presto deployment, so the benchmark code is not public and no compiler or CPU model is given.
