name: Crystal (GPU query-processing library)
baseline: OmniSci (commercial GPU OLAP DBMS, formerly MapD, now HEAVY.AI) on the same GPU. Also the authors' own equivalent CPU implementation, which is itself compared against Hyper and MonetDB.
workload: 13 Star Schema Benchmark queries at scale factor 20 (120M-row lineorder fact table, about 13 GB). String columns are dictionary-encoded to 4-byte integers and the queries are manually rewritten. Data is preloaded into device memory, and each result is the average of 3 runs. Crystal on the GPU (thread block 256, 8 items per thread per tile) is compared with OmniSci on the GPU and with an equivalent CPU implementation; Hyper and MonetDB are compared only with that CPU implementation.
claimed_speedup: Per the SIGMOD 2020 paper (Section 5.2): the Crystal-based Standalone GPU implementation is on average about 16x faster than OmniSci (a commercial GPU OLAP DBMS) on the same V100, and on average 25x faster than the authors' own equivalent CPU implementation across the 13 SSB queries. The 1.17x (vs Hyper) and 2.5x (vs MonetDB) averages belong to the authors' Standalone CPU implementation, not to Crystal on the GPU. The paper does not state direct GPU-vs-Hyper or GPU-vs-MonetDB ratios.
compiler_and_flags: GPU: nvcc (CUDA 10.0). The repo Makefile compiles with -O3 --std=c++11 -Xptxas="-dlcm=cg" and defaults to gencode sm_52 (the sm_70 lines are commented out). CPU-implementation compiler and flags are not stated.
hardware: CPU: single-socket Intel i7-6900 (the paper calls it Skylake-class; 8 cores/16 SMT, AVX2, 64 GB). GPU: Nvidia V100 (32 GB, 880 GB/s; measured bidirectional PCIe 12.8 GB/s). Ubuntu 16.04, CUDA 10.0.
tradeoffs: Requires an Nvidia GPU and CUDA toolchain; provides block-wide device-function building blocks and SSB query implementations rather than a full SQL engine; the paper's own cost analysis weighs the ~$3/hr V100 rental cost against the speedup rather than declaring an unconditional win.
caveats: The headline GPU speedups are largely cross-hardware: a V100 against an 8-core desktop CPU, a memory-bandwidth ratio of about 16x. The paper is a GPU-vs-CPU study; the like-for-like incumbent comparison is Crystal vs OmniSci on the same GPU (about 16x). Hyper and MonetDB were compared only against the authors' CPU implementation. The CPU implementation and the baseline-system runs are not in the repo. The ~13 GB SF20 dataset fits in GPU memory. Published at SIGMOD 2020, so it predates DuckDB/ClickHouse-era baselines. The last commit on master (the only branch) is 2020-08-29; the 2024-06-03 date is GitHub's pushed_at, not a commit. It is an academic reference library.

name: Lance
baseline: Apache Parquet (the parquet-rs Rust crate, tuned, in the paper). Iceberg is named only in the README/homepage marketing and is not benchmarked in the paper.
workload: Paper (arXiv 2504.15247): parallel 'take' operations of 256 random indices from a single column, run for 10 s and reported as rows fetched per second, over 8 data types (UInt64 scalars through 100 KiB image lists) with 10% nulls. Small types use about 1 billion rows. Parquet uses 8 KiB pages with compression and dictionary encoding off. Full-scan, compression-ratio and struct-packing experiments are also included. All runs are on local NVMe.
claimed_speedup: README/homepage marketing: '100x faster random access than Parquet or Iceberg'. The README's 'Vs. parquet' section attributes this to a preliminary Oxford Pet dataset test ('For batched random access, Lance is 100x better than both parquet and raw files'). The paper (arXiv 2504.15247) states instead that Parquet 'when configured correctly, can achieve over 60x better random access performance than default settings' (parquet-rs default 5,500 rows/s vs optimized 350,000 rows/s on small scalars). It also says the Lance 2.1 encoding 'generally tie[s] or beat[s] Parquet' in random access without the scan-performance and RAM trade-offs, but gives no single speedup figure against tuned Parquet.
hardware: Samsung 970 EVO Plus 2TB NVMe drive (measured 850K random 4KiB reads/s, 3,400 MiB/s) with an Intel i7-10700K CPU (8 cores/16 threads), per the paper
tradeoffs: Rust-native with Python/Java bindings (pylance); optimized for AI/ML lakehouse workloads (multimodal blobs, vector indexes, data versioning) rather than general OLAP scans; file format still evolving under a data_storage_version compatibility contract.
caveats: The '100x faster than Parquet or Iceberg' figure comes from README/homepage copy, backed only by a 'preliminary' Oxford Pet dataset test without methodology. The paper, written by LanceDB employees, undercuts it by showing tuned Parquet recovers over 60x versus default Parquet, and it claims only tie-or-beat against tuned Parquet. Lance 2.1 slightly underperforms Lance 2.0 on simple scalar types. The project homepage says the paper was published at VLDB 2025, but arXiv v1 carries no journal reference and a crossref title search found no match, so peer review is unconfirmed. The paper mentions reproduction scripts but gives no link. The paper's metric is throughput (rows/s) rather than latency.
found_via: gh api repos/lance-format/lance; WebFetch lance.org homepage; arXiv abstract 2504.15247

verification.tier_reason: The arXiv paper by LanceDB authors compares Lance 2.1 random access against tuned parquet-rs on stated hardware (i7-10700K, Samsung 970 EVO Plus). In the text it reports only that Lance 'generally tie[s] or beat[s] Parquet', with no stated ratio. The 100x headline comes only from first-party README/homepage copy without methodology. Peer review (VLDB '25) is claimed by the project homepage but could not be confirmed, and neither compiler/flags nor a linked script path is given, so the tier is C.
verification.notes: Metadata is confirmed: Apache-2.0, 7,117 stars, last commit 2026-09-26, not a fork. The record's 'metric: latency' is really throughput (rows/s) in the paper; metric is not a correctable field. The tier stays C.

The peer-reviewed VLDB 2025 paper is more nuanced: its own abstract states 'Parquet, when configured correctly, can achieve over 60x better random access performance than default settings' -- i.e. most of the headline 100x gap is against Parquet's poorly-tuned defaults, not a well-tuned Parquet baseline; Lance's actual claimed contribution is matching/exceeding well-tuned Parquet's random access without giving up scan throughput or RAM usage.
corrected_fields.workload: Random-access point lookups and full-scan throughput on NVMe-backed storage, per the VLDB 2025 paper 'Lance: Efficient Random Access in Columnar Storage through Adaptive Structural Encodings' (hardware: NVMe drive + Intel i7-10700K, 8 cores/16 threads).

name: Sirius
workload: TPC-H benchmark (22 queries) hot runs at scale factors SF100/300/500/1000 (100GB-1TB), Sirius (a GPU execution engine plugged into DuckDB via Substrait) vs plain DuckDB on CPU
claimed_speedup: 5.5x faster at SF100 (1.71s vs 9.37s), 5.7x at SF300 (4.48s vs 25.72s), 5.2x at SF500 (8.14s vs 42.25s), 2.7x at SF1000 (31.79s vs 85.91s); also 2.1x-5.3x cheaper per run
hardware: Sirius (GPU): best of AWS g7e.2xlarge/4xlarge/8xlarge per scale factor (which size won at each SF is not stated), NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96GB; DuckDB (CPU) v1.5.5: AWS Graviton5 m9g.16xlarge
tradeoffs: Requires an NVIDIA GPU (Turing+, CUDA 12.x/13.x) and Linux with io_uring enabled; plugs into DuckDB via Substrait and falls back silently to CPU for unsupported operators; only DuckDB is a supported target today (StarRocks integration planned)
caveats: First-party benchmark read from a README chart PNG (docs/super-sirius-perf.png); there is no raw results table, and no compiler/build flags are stated. These are hot runs only, and the Sirius time is the best of three g7e instance sizes. The hardware is asymmetric: an RTX PRO 6000 96GB GPU instance against a Graviton5 m9g.16xlarge CPU instance. The chart partly normalizes for this by reporting cost per run (Sirius 2.1-5.3x cheaper). The speedup shrinks from 5.5x at SF100 to 2.7x at SF1000. The page gives no reason, so the earlier explanation (GPU memory/bandwidth bottleneck) is speculation.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "sirius GPU DuckDB"; gh api repos/sirius-db/sirius

name: StarRocks
workload: Star Schema Benchmark flattened into a single wide table (SSB-Flat, 100 GB; the ClickHouse-style denormalized SSB, so no joins), 13 queries, 1 warm-up plus the average of 3 runs. StarRocks 3.5.0 vs ClickHouse 25.3.3.42 (and Apache Druid 33.0.0), all with default configurations.
claimed_speedup: StarRocks docs (SSB Flat-table Benchmarking): on 13 queries over the 100 GB SSB-Flat dataset, 'StarRocks has an overall query performance 1.87x that of ClickHouse' (sum of average latencies 992 ms vs 1,858 ms; per-query ratios 1.12x-2.63x). The earlier StarRocks blog post (Aug 21, 2023; https://www.starrocks.io/blog/benchmark-test) claimed 'ClickHouse has a response time 2.2x slower than that of StarRocks' on the same 13 SSB flat-table queries, with no hardware stated.
hardware: AWS m7i.4xlarge hosts (16 vCPU, 64 GiB each; 5 instances listed). StarRocks runs 1 FE + 3 BEs and ClickHouse 3 nodes. CPU model and OS not stated.
tradeoffs: MPP architecture with a separate Java frontend (FE, planner/metadata) and C++ backend (BE, vectorized execution engine) -- heavier operational footprint than embedded engines like DuckDB; MySQL-wire compatible.
caveats: These are vendor-run numbers: default configs, no CPU model, no compiler flags and no linked benchmark scripts. The 2023 blog gave 2.2x; the current docs give 1.87x (StarRocks 3.5.0 vs ClickHouse 25.3.3.42). The claim is contradicted by the independent ClickBench suite on identical single-node c6a.4xlarge hardware. There, ClickHouse's 2026-09-26 run sums to 18.03 s (best of 3 across 43 queries) versus 44.47 s for StarRocks' 2026-09-07 run, so ClickHouse is about 2.5x faster (derived from page data: ClickHouse/ClickBench clickhouse/results/20260926/c6a.4xlarge.json vs starrocks/results/20260907/c6a.4xlarge.json). Both the vendor SSB-Flat test and ClickBench are single-flat-table workloads, not star-schema joins, so the gap cannot be put down to join handling. It more likely reflects cluster vs single-node setup, dataset and query mix, and tuning. The win should be treated as workload- and setup-specific.
found_via: gh api repos/StarRocks/starrocks/contents/README.md; WebFetch starrocks.io/blog/benchmark-test; ClickHouse/ClickBench GitHub repo

The current StarRocks docs page reports 1.87x with instance types, versions and per-query latencies, but gives no CPU model, compiler/flags or public benchmark script, so it is C, not A/B.
verification.notes: Both the 2023 blog's 2.2x and the ClickBench 18.03 s vs 44.47 s figures were verified. The record's caveat wrongly calls the vendor test 'star-schema joins': it is SSB flat tables. benchmark_url was switched to the current docs page, which states instance type, versions and per-query data (1.87x); the old blog is kept in claimed_speedup/caveats. The orchestrator may want to flag this as contested given the independent ClickBench reversal.

corrected_fields.workload: Star Schema Benchmark (SSB), 13 queries on flat tables (vendor blog post dated Aug 21, 2023)

It is directly CONTRADICTED by ClickHouse's own independent, reproducible ClickBench suite: on identical c6a.4xlarge hardware, ClickHouse's 2026-09-26 run totals 18.03s (sum of best-of-3 across the 43 ClickBench queries) versus StarRocks' 2026-09-07 run at 44.47s -- i.e. ClickHouse is now roughly 2.5x FASTER than StarRocks on ClickBench, the reverse of the vendor's SSB claim (derived from page data: ClickHouse/ClickBench GitHub repo, clickhouse/results/20260926/c6a.4xlarge.json vs starrocks/results/20260907/c6a.4xlarge.json). The discrepancy likely reflects ~3 years of ClickHouse improvements plus workload differences (SSB star-schema joins vs. ClickBench's flat-table scans), but it substantially weakens confidence in the vendor claim as a current, general statement.

name: Vortex
workload: First-party CI benchmark dashboard (bench.vortex.dev) covering write and scan throughput (compress-bench), hot and cold random-access take latency over taxi, feature-vectors, nested-lists and nested-structs datasets, ClickBench, TPC-H SF1/10/100 on NVMe and S3, TPC-DS SF1 and others. Each workload runs with both DataFusion and DuckDB as the query engine, against Parquet, Lance, Arrow IPC and DuckDB native formats.
claimed_speedup: bench.vortex.dev (live page, build 737386b as of 2026-09-26). Two figures are geomean throughput ratios to Parquet: write throughput 2.97x (1,756 vs 605 MB/s) and scan throughput 30.73x (84.14 vs 3.20 GB/s). The page's other summary ratios are geomean time ratios to the fastest entry (lower is better), not speedups over Parquet. Random access, hot: Vortex 1.15x (1.85 ms) vs Parquet 627.08x (65.32 s), about 545x (derived from page data). Random access, cold: Vortex 1.35x (3.31 ms) vs Parquet 432.76x (67.10 s), about 321x (derived from page data). ClickBench: DataFusion+Vortex 3.99 s vs DataFusion+Parquet 6.08 s, about 1.52x (derived from page data); DuckDB+Vortex 4.65 s vs DuckDB+Parquet 5.45 s, about 1.17x (derived from page data). TPC-H SF1 NVMe: DuckDB+Vortex 450.40 ms vs DuckDB+Parquet 1.51 s, about 3.35x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the page. Per the repo's CI workflow: rustc 1.98.0 (rust-toolchain.toml), RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native -C force-frame-pointers=yes', cargo --profile release_debug.
hardware: Not stated on the page. The repo's CI workflows (.github/workflows/develop-bench.yml, sql-bench-matrix.yml) run benchmarks on an AWS EC2 c8gd.metal-24xl (ARM64); no CPU model is named.
stars_or_usage: 3,225 stars; LF AI & Data incubation-stage project
tradeoffs: Rust-native (needs FFI/bindings for direct C++ use, though it advertises zero-copy Arrow compatibility); file format only reached 'stable' status from v0.36.0 onward; young ecosystem versus Parquet's universal tooling support.
caveats: First-party dashboard whose numbers change with every commit. Most summary 'x' figures are geomean ratios to the fastest entry, not speedups over Parquet, so only the write and scan throughput ratios are direct Parquet comparisons. On the same page, results on S3 are mixed. At TPC-H S3 SF1, DataFusion+Parquet is fastest (6.54 s vs DataFusion+Vortex 8.86 s). At TPC-H S3 SF100, DuckDB+Vortex takes 488.62 s vs 73.45 s for DuckDB+Parquet. The independent ClickHouse/ClickBench results (c6a.4xlarge, sum of best-of-3 over 43 queries, derived from the result JSONs) are also mixed. On 2026-05-11, duckdb-vortex took 40.99 s vs 32.48 s for duckdb-parquet: slower in total because one query is about 20x slower, though it was faster on 26 of 43 queries and about 5% faster by geomean. A 'tuned' duckdb-vortex run on 2026-09-26 took 29.69 s but loaded in 762 s. On 2026-08-20, DataFusion+Vortex took 91.30 s vs 45.57 s for DataFusion+Parquet and was about 1.37x slower by geomean. That contradicts the dashboard's DataFusion ClickBench win, although the engine versions differ (Vortex CLI on DataFusion 53.1.0, Parquet run on 54.0.0). The huge random-access ratios mostly reflect Parquet having no row-level random access.
found_via: gh api repos/vortex-data/vortex; WebFetch of bench.vortex.dev; ClickHouse/ClickBench GitHub repo (duckdb-vortex and duckdb-parquet results/20260511/c6a.4xlarge.json)

verification.tier_reason: bench.vortex.dev is Vortex's own CI dashboard. It compares against Parquet, and the benchmark code is public (benchmarks/compress-bench, random-access-bench, datafusion-bench, duckdb-bench). The page names no hardware or flags. The CI workflows give an AWS instance type (c8gd.metal-24xl), RUSTFLAGS and rustc 1.98.0, but no CPU model, so per precedent this is first-party C.
verification.notes: The record misread the dashboard. Its 1.13x (ClickBench) and 1.32x (TPC-H) figures are ratio-to-fastest scores, not speedups over Parquet, and the Parquet 65.32 s random-access figure is from the hot panel, not a cold/hot mix. I rewrote claimed_speedup with the direct comparisons, marked as derived. I downgraded because the query-engine wins over Parquet are contested by independent ClickBench results, including a new DataFusion+Vortex result that is 2x slower in total. The write and scan throughput wins stand, first-party only.

name: ArceKV (ElasticLSM + Arce)
workload: Dynamic and static read/write-ratio workloads on a RocksDB-based KV store, cgroup-capped memory (75GiB), comparing against RocksDB's own Leveling/1-Leveling/Tiering compaction styles and academic baselines (LazyLeveling, Moose, Ruskey, CAMAL)
claimed_speedup: Paper: average 2.00x and 1.41x over 1-Leveling (RocksDB's default compaction style, the strongest baseline) across the two dynamic workloads; 2.17x-2.92x over Tiering and LazyLeveling; around 3x faster than state-of-the-art compaction strategies in dynamic scenarios; over 10x vs Cassandra and WiredTiger and 3x vs Pebble. Repo README (prod branch, in-memory tmpfs variant vs RocksDB leveling): total latency 282.09s vs 808.85s at read_ratio 0.1 (2.87x) shrinking to 438.04s vs 479.20s at 0.9 (1.09x) (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in paper; repo README lists gcc/g++ (version unstated) with a CMake Release build
hardware: Intel Core i9-13900K (5.40GHz), 128GB RAM, 1TB NVMe SSD, Ubuntu 22.04, ext4, memory capped at 75GiB via cgroup
license: GPL-2.0 (GitHub-detected; repo is a modified RocksDB tree that ships both LICENSE.Apache and LICENSE.leveldb, matching RocksDB's dual Apache-2.0/GPL-2.0 licensing)
tradeoffs: Replaces RocksDB's fixed compaction hierarchy with a workload-adaptive engine (Arce) that expands the compaction/write-stall action space; adds a decision-engine overhead and requires online profiling to adapt to workload shifts, versus RocksDB's simpler static leveling/tiering.
caveats: The paper states no compiler or flags. The 1-Leveling/Leveling/Tiering/LazyLeveling baselines were implemented on the RocksDB-based Moose framework, not stock RocksDB builds. Stock RocksDB appears only in the industrial-system comparison. The default 'prod' branch is explicitly NOT a faithful implementation of the paper: it is an in-memory adaptation for a TikTok recommendation service. An on-disk version was published on the 'dev' branch (2026-04-29), and its README reports a modest gain over leveled compaction: 1.41x total runtime (929.0s vs 1310.5s) and about 10% lower all-op latency, with worse insert latency (2.45us vs 2.15us) and higher compaction I/O. The prod README's cmake line has a typo (-CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE). License: GitHub detects GPL-2.0; the tree carries RocksDB's COPYING (GPLv2), LICENSE.Apache and LICENSE.leveldb.
found_via: arXiv API query all:key-value+store+AND+all:outperform+AND+all:RocksDB -> arxiv.org/abs/2508.03565; code located in paper text (github.com/NTU-Siqiang-Group/ArceKV)

The tier drops from A to B because no compiler or flags are stated anywhere. The public default branch differs from the evaluated system, so treat the repo as a research artifact.

name: DobLIX
workload: SOSD real-world (WIKI, AMZN, FB, OSM) and synthetic (LOGN, UNI) datasets, 64M pairs with 8-byte keys and 64-byte values; RO/RH/BA/WH read-write mixes plus YCSB A-F macrobenchmarks on RocksDB 8.1.1 (per paper), 4 background threads
claimed_speedup: Average throughput vs stock RocksDB indexing: 2.21x on read-only (RO), 1.22x read-heavy, 1.31x balanced, 1.04x write-heavy; vs TridentKV/Bourbon on RO: 1.41x/1.57x. YCSB B/C/D average 2.02x vs RocksDB; YCSB-E +42.8%. +81% vs RocksDB at 512MB cache (RO, Zipfian, AMZN). RO tail latency 2.13x better than RocksDB. Abstract: 1.19x-2.21x vs state-of-the-art methods within RocksDB. The '2.67x' figure is TridentKV's tail latency relative to DobLIX, not a throughput gain over RocksDB.

license: BSD-3-Clause (RocksDB 5.x-era 'BSD License For rocksdb software' LICENSE text; GitHub reports NOASSERTION) plus Facebook PATENTS file (Additional Grant of Patent Rights Version 2)
tradeoffs: Adds a dual-objective learned index (RadixSpline-based) plus an RL agent for tuning block size/error bound on top of RocksDB; extra training/tuning overhead; RL agent adds runtime complexity vs stock RocksDB.
caveats: GitHub shows NOASSERTION. The LICENSE is RocksDB's old BSD-3-Clause text, shipped with Facebook's PATENTS grant (v2) and its termination clause. The public repo is a RocksDB 5.1.2 tree (include/rocksdb/version.h) with a learned_index/ directory, but the paper evaluates on RocksDB 8.1.1. name: PsiTri (arbtrie)
workload: TPC-B-style bank-transfer benchmark. Each transfer is one atomic transaction of 5 KV ops (2 reads, 2 updates, 1 insert), with triangular-skew access and a fixed seed. The main runs use 1M accounts, 10M transfer attempts, 100 transfers per commit and sync=none. The PsiTriRocks drop-in comparison is a separate April 2026 EPYC run: 1M accounts, 1M transactions, batch=1, sync=none, write-only and write plus one concurrent reader.
claimed_speedup: PsiTriRocks (RocksDB-API drop-in) vs RocksDB, April 2026 AMD EPYC-Turin, batch=1: 2.3x write throughput (369,446 vs 157,588 transfers/sec) and 4.9x reader throughput under concurrent writes (1,416,652 vs 289,627 reads/sec). Native PsiTri vs RocksDB in the batch=100 run: 376,691 vs 126,341 transfers/sec on Apple M5 Max, about 2.98x (derived from page data); 163,614 vs 104,102 transfers/sec on AMD EPYC-Turin, about 1.57x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Apple M5 Max: Clang 17, C++20, -O3 -flto=thin. AMD EPYC-Turin: Clang 20, C++20, -O3 -flto -march=native (AVX-512 enabled)

name: CompassDB
workload: YCSB A-F with 16 threads after loading 200M keys (20-byte keys, 1KB values) then 100M operations; O_DIRECT, compression disabled, RocksDB/PebblesDB with 32MB LRU block cache, up to 4x128MB memtables; plus Workload C value-size sweep (50B-50KB) and fill/read/mixed microbenchmarks
claimed_speedup: YCSB (16 threads, 200M keys, 100M ops): 2.5x-4x throughput vs RocksDB and 5x-17x vs PebblesDB on point-lookup/insert workloads A, B, C, D, F. Workload A ~3x, C 2.52x, D 5.5x vs RocksDB. 50%-85% lower average/p99 latency vs RocksDB. Slower than both RocksDB and PebblesDB on scan-heavy YCSB-E. Intro: RocksDB's write amplification about 2x CompassDB's (15x in a 100M-key one-level test), read amplification 3x in pure reads, space amplification 1.2x.
benchmark_url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18099 (arXiv v1 preprint, 26 Jun 2024; no journal reference listed)
hardware: Dell PowerEdge T440, Intel Xeon Silver 2.40 GHz (exact model not stated), Samsung PM9A3 3.84TB NVMe SSD, 128GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, ext4 (ordered mode)
tradeoffs: Perfect-hash in-memory index (~6 bytes/KV) instead of RocksDB's default block-based index+bloom filter; claims RocksDB API compatibility for drop-in migration, but no public implementation to verify; perfect-hash structures typically complicate/limit fully dynamic online rebuilds under skewed insert patterns.
caveats: No public repository: GitHub search finds only unrelated 'compassdb' projects. The arXiv preprint (v1, June 2024) has no venue or journal reference. The claimed SIGMOD / Proc. ACM Manag. Data 3(6) Article 294 publication could not be verified: there is no CompassDB entry in Crossref's PACMMOD (ISSN 2836-6573) index, even though vol 3 issue 6 is indexed. The authors are all from DiPeak, the vendor, so these are first-party numbers. The secondary baseline is PebblesDB, not SplinterDB; SplinterDB appears only as related work. Setup is not like-for-like: RocksDB/PebblesDB got a 32MB block cache under O_DIRECT, and CompassDB loses on scan-heavy YCSB-E.

name: DiaLSM
workload: db_bench FillRandom (128B/1KB/8KB values, 10M entries per I/O thread) and ReadRandomWriteRandom (100M 1KB entries preloaded); YCSB A-F with 1KB values; Sysbench OLTP on MariaDB/MyRocks. DiaLSM is built atop RocksDB v8.3.2. Baselines are RocksDB v8.3.2 with Sub-Compaction, and ADOC. For all systems, write throttling (WST), commit logging and block cache were disabled.
claimed_speedup: 8KB FillRandom: up to 2.4x higher throughput and ~50% lower latency than ADOC (a RocksDB-based auto-tuner), not stock RocksDB. 94.3% fewer write stalls: ADOC and RocksDB show up to 17.6x higher stall rates. ~50% lower average/median latency than both RocksDB(16) and ADOC(16) (Fig. 7). ReadRandomWriteRandom: 1.8x vs ADOC. YCSB-E: ~1.7x vs ADOC and RocksDB at the default scan length 128, and 3.3x/5.7x/8.9x at scan lengths 1K/4K/16K; YCSB-C at parity. Sysbench on MariaDB/MyRocks: 2.3x vs ADOC on oltp_insert, up to 9.9x on oltp_write_only, 2.2x vs ADOC on oltp_read_write.
hardware: Two AMD EPYC 7352 24-core CPUs, 256GB RAM, MZSLR3T8HBLS-00A07 NVMe SSD, CentOS 7 with ext4
tradeoffs: Shards the write-flush-compaction pipeline internally to avoid a single monolithic stall path; adds shard-management complexity and per-shard resource overhead.
caveats: Venue is author-reported only. The arXiv comment (v1, 2026-09-13) and the repo README say the paper was accepted to the 43rd IEEE ICDE 2027 (Copenhagen, May 17-21 2027). The date fits ICDE 2027's Round-1 notification (2026-09-10), but there is no public accepted-papers list or proceedings, so peer review cannot be confirmed yet. Tier is held at C; it can go to B once ICDE 2027 lists the paper. The headline 2.4x/1.8x/2.2x/2.3x gains are against ADOC, not stock RocksDB. Against RocksDB the paper shows ~50% lower latency, 94.3% fewer stalls and the YCSB-E range-scan wins. The RocksDB config is non-default: throttling, WAL/commit logging and block cache were all disabled. The paper says the code is 'publicly available' at DISCOS-LAB/DiaLSM, but the repo holds only a README ('will be available soon') and has no license. Compiler/flags are not stated.

name: F2 (FASTER v2)
workload: YCSB (A/B/C/D/F/W) and MixGraph benchmarks, 250M keys (8B key/100B value), Zipfian skew, on CloudLab NVMe RAID-0, memory budget 10% of dataset size
claimed_speedup: 2-11.9x better throughput than existing KV stores (abstract). Fig. 10 (YCSB + MixGraph, 16 cores, memory = 10% of dataset) averages: 11.8x RocksDB v8.11.4, 2.1x FASTER, 2x LeanStore, 4.6x SplinterDB, 11.9x KVell. Average request latency vs RocksDB: 1.4x lower read and 3.5x lower write (Table 1).
hardware: CloudLab sm110p node: 16-core Intel Xeon Silver 4314, 128GiB RAM, 4x Samsung PM9A3 NVMe SSD (PCIe 4.0) in RAID-0, Linux kernel 5.4, ext4
tradeoffs: Two-tier hash-index + record-log design optimized for skewed, larger-than-memory workloads; latch-free multi-threaded compaction adds implementation complexity; tuned for direct I/O with WAL/compression/checksums disabled in the benchmark, which is not RocksDB's typical durable-by-default configuration.
caveats: The paper is PVLDB 18(12):4910-4923, 2025 (VLDB 2025, doi:10.14778/3750601.3750615), not VLDB 2023; 2023 is the arXiv v1 date. The 11.8x RocksDB average covers YCSB and MixGraph, not YCSB alone. The latency win is 1.4x on reads and 3.5x on writes, not 3.5x on both. All systems ran with Direct I/O and with WAL/persistence, compression and checksums disabled (non-default). RocksDB was further tuned with 10-bit Bloom filters and the data-block hash index via OptimizeForPointLookup(). Memory was capped at 10% of dataset (3GiB YCSB, 4GiB MixGraph). F2's benchmark code is public (cc/benchmark-dir/benchmark_f2.cc; Release builds with -O3 -g), but the compiler/version is unstated and the RocksDB harness is not in the repo, so the tier stays B.

name: KVell
workload: YCSB core workloads (uniform and Zipfian key distributions), 1024B items, 100GB(100M keys)/5TB(5B keys) synthetic datasets, plus two Nutanix write-heavy (57:41:2 write:read:scan) production workloads, 250B-1KB items.
claimed_speedup: Abstract: throughput at least 2x the closest competitor (RocksDB 6.2, PebblesDB, TokuMX, WiredTiger) on read-dominated workloads and 5x on write-dominated workloads; on mostly-scan workloads comparable or better; maximum latencies an order of magnitude lower than the best competitor, even on scan-based workloads. Body (Config-Optane, 100M 1KB items): YCSB A 8x RocksDB and 5.8x PebblesDB (next best); YCSB B/C 2.2x/2.7x over existing KVs; Nutanix production workloads ~4x RocksDB (the next best); uniform YCSB E roughly equal to RocksDB (13.9K vs 14.4K scans/s).
compiler_and_flags: Paper states none. Repo Makefile defaults: clang with CFLAGS=-O2 -ggdb3 -Wall (clang++ -std=c++11 for index code); README recommends TCMalloc (gperftools). Not confirmed as the build used for the paper runs.
hardware: Config-SSD: 32-core 2.4GHz Intel Xeon, 128GB RAM, 480GB Intel DC S3500 SSD; Config-Amazon-8NVMe: AWS i3.metal, 36x2 (72) cores at 2.3GHz, 488GB RAM, 8x1.9TB NVMe SSDs; Config-Optane: 4-core 4.2GHz Intel i7, 60GB RAM, 480GB Intel Optane 905P
tradeoffs: Shared-nothing architecture can suffer load imbalance; no in-memory sorted global index so scans are relatively weaker; designed around 4KB-atomic-write SSDs.
caveats: Peer-reviewed SOSP'19 paper. The paper states no compiler or flags, and the repo Makefile defaults to clang -O2. CPU models are not named. The repo reproduces only the KVell side (scripts/run-aws.sh, sample_results); the RocksDB/PebblesDB/TokuMX/WiredTiger runs have no published harness. Scans are weaker: RocksDB wins with small items, and uniform YCSB E is about equal (13.9K vs 14.4K scans/s). The latest commit (2025-12-15) only fixes random-number generation in a workload generator; before that the last commit was 2020-11, and the 'osdi' branch holds KVell+ (OSDI'20).

name: MatrixKV
workload: db_bench micro-benchmarks: 80GB of KV pairs (16B keys, 4KB default values, 64B-64KB sweep) inserted in uniform random order, then sequential writes and random/sequential reads; YCSB load plus workloads A-F (80GB load, 1M ops each); tail latency from YCSB-A at ~20K req/s. Each hybrid store limited to 8GB NVM, with RocksDB defaults (64MB memtable, 256MB L1, AF 10).
claimed_speedup: Abstract: 3.6x higher random-write throughput and 5x lower 99th-percentile latency than RocksDB (2.6x / 1.9x vs NoveLSM). Paper body: random-write throughput (db_bench, 80GB, 4KB values) is 3.6x RocksDB-L0-NVM (RocksDB with an 8GB L0 in NVM; 1.86x-3.61x across 64B-64KB values) and 2.6x NoveLSM; YCSB load 3.29x RocksDB-L0-NVM. YCSB-A p99 latency (Table 2: 405us vs 786/2080/11055us) is 1.9x lower than RocksDB-L0-NVM, 5x lower than NoveLSM, and 27x lower than stock RocksDB-SSD, so the abstract's latency pairing is swapped relative to the body.
hardware: Two Intel 2.20GHz 24-core processors (model not named), 32GB DRAM, 800GB Intel SSDSC2BB800G7 SSD, 2x128GB Intel Optane DC PMM (8GB NVM used per store); Fedora 27, Linux 4.13.9
tradeoffs: Requires Intel Optane/PMDK-class NVM hardware to realize the reported gains; not a plain-SSD design.

name: SpanDB
workload: LSM-tree KV store on hybrid storage, SpanDB vs vanilla RocksDB v6.5.1: YCSB all-write, A, B, E and F (Zipfian and uniform) on a 512 GB database, plus LinkBench, across three capacity-disk/speed-disk pairs (S-N2, S-O, N1-O). SpanDB writes its WAL via SPDK to the fast NVMe disk; RocksDB writes WAL to the same disk via ext4.
claimed_speedup: 'improves RocksDB's throughput by up to 8.8x and reduces its latency by 9.5-58.3%' (FAST'21 abstract). The 8.8x peak comes from the YCSB all-write workload (20M Zipfian writes: 7.6-8.8x across device pairs). The read-heavy YCSB-B/E gains are only 1.03-1.66x in throughput.
hardware: 2x 20-core Intel Xeon Gold 6248, 256 GB DRAM, CentOS 7.7; Intel Optane P4800X, P4510 and P4610 NVMe SSDs, plus S4510 SATA SSDs in 4+1 RAID5, tested as capacity-disk/speed-disk pairs
tradeoffs: Requires SPDK plus manual NVMe setup (hugepages, unbinding devices from the kernel driver), a much heavier deployment than plain RocksDB. Built by adapting the RocksDB codebase (not flagged as a GitHub fork, but derived from it) to place WAL and top LSM levels on faster NVMe.
caveats: The baseline is RocksDB v6.5.1 (2019). The paper does not state the compiler version or flags. SpanDB needs SPDK, hugepages and a dedicated NVMe device for the WAL, and its gains are largest on write-intensive workloads (read-heavy YCSB-B/E gives 1.03-1.66x). The repo has had no commits since August 2023, so it is an unmaintained research prototype.

name: BVLSM
workload: db_bench random and sequential writes with 4KB-64KB values under sync, async and disabled WAL (R-WS/R-WA/R-WO, S-WS/S-WA/S-WO); YCSB workload A (16B keys, 8KB values, 500k preloaded records); 100GB sustained random-write stability test. Baselines are RocksDB v9.7.3 and BlobDB. The comparison is WAL-time vs flush-time key-value separation.
claimed_speedup: 64KB random writes: 7.6x throughput vs RocksDB v9.7.3 and 1.9x vs BlobDB with async WAL (R-WA); ~7x vs RocksDB and ~3x vs BlobDB with sync WAL (R-WS); up to 8x vs RocksDB and 2x vs BlobDB with WAL off (R-WO). Sequential writes: S-WS ~4.1x RocksDB / 9.8x BlobDB, S-WA ~1.3x / 2.2x, S-WO up to 1.3x / 2x. YCSB-A (8KB values): insert/update/read latency is 27.2%/28.4%/19.7% of RocksDB's. 100GB sustained random write: 1.5x RocksDB and 2x BlobDB on average.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 5218 (16C/32T, 2.30GHz), 4x32GB DDR4-2933 (128GB), Samsung 990 EVO NVMe SSD (1TB), Ubuntu 20.04
tradeoffs: Separates key/value at WAL-write time rather than at flush time so MemTables only hold lightweight metadata; adds a multi-queue BValue store and BVCache; targets big-value (multimedia/embedding) workloads specifically, smaller advantage expected for small-value workloads typical of many RocksDB deployments.
caveats: Peer-reviewed: published in the 2025 IEEE International Conference on High Performance Computing and Communications (HPCC 2025, Exeter UK, Aug 13-15 2025), pp. 34-41, doi:10.1109/HPCC67675.2025.00037. This was found via Crossref; the arXiv page has no journal-ref. No public code repository exists (a GitHub search for BVLSM returns only an unrelated spam repo), and compiler/flags are not stated, so it cannot reach tier A. All numbers are the authors' own. The earlier '~7x and 3x over RocksDB' was a misreading: under sync WAL it is ~7x over RocksDB and ~3x over BlobDB.

name: CalicoDB
workload: LevelDB db_bench adapted to CalicoDB and SQLite (fillseq, fillseqsync, fillseqbatch, fillrandom, fillrandsync, fillrandbatch, overwrite, overwritebatch, readrandom, readseq, fillrand100K, fillseq100K, readseq100K, readrand100K), run in CI on GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest and macos-latest. CalicoDB 0.0.1 (commit 30fe767) vs SQLite3 3.39.5. SQLite was configured with a WITHOUT ROWID table, WAL mode, 4 KiB pages, synchronous=NORMAL (FULL for the *sync benchmarks) and EXCLUSIVE locking.
claimed_speedup: Latency in microseconds per op, CalicoDB 0.0.1 vs SQLite3 3.39.5. readrand100K: 58.801 vs 252.367 on Linux (~4.3x, derived from page data) and 79.160 vs 495.537 on macOS (~6.3x, derived). readseq100K: 58.518 vs 89.065 on Linux (~1.5x, derived) and 74.773 vs 203.458 on macOS (~2.7x, derived). fillseqbatch: 1.040 vs 2.033 on Linux (~2.0x, derived). fillseq: 23.056 vs 29.767 on Linux (~1.3x, derived). Results are mixed. On Linux CalicoDB is slower on fillrandom, fillrandbatch, overwrite, overwritebatch, readrandom (4.613 vs 4.270) and fillrand100K. On macOS it is slower on fillrandom, fillrandbatch, overwrite and overwritebatch, and much slower on fillseqsync (1101.377 vs 291.237, ~3.8x slower) and fillrandsync (1117.884 vs 213.655, ~5.2x slower) because it uses F_FULLFSYNC.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (version and flags unstated)
hardware: GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest / macos-latest runners (exact CPU model unstated)
tradeoffs: Results are mixed rather than a clean win: faster on sequential writes and large random-read batches, slower on plain random writes/overwrites. Tiny, low-visibility project (43 stars).
caveats: Benchmarked on generic CI runners with no CPU model and no stated compiler version or flags, so it falls short of Tier A despite public benchmark code. The author's disclaimer says SQLite is an RDBMS with more per-operation overhead than a KV store, and the README says CalicoDB is 'not ready for production'. The results are for an old commit (30fe767). Wins are concentrated in large-value (100K) reads and sequential or batched fills; CalicoDB is slower on random and overwrite writes, and several times slower on the macOS *sync benchmarks. name: Mycelium (TE-LSM)
workload: RocksDB-based prototype that embeds split, convert (JSON to FlatBuffers) and augment (secondary index) transformations into compaction through cross-column-family 'Tierveling'. Measured: write throughput after a 100 GB preload (200M records of about 500 B), plus query latency (min/P25/P50/P75/max) for Q2 to Q7 (column-retrieving, row-retrieving and index point/range queries) with Zipfian keys, against RocksDB baselines.
claimed_speedup: Up to 4.25x lower query latency (abstract: 'up to 425% improvements in read latency compared to RocksDB baseline') for Q2, a column-retrieving range query (max over a range). This is with the CONVERT transformer (JSON to FlatBuffers during compaction) against a RocksDB baseline that stores JSON. The split transformation gives 2.8x on Q2, and row-retrieving queries (Q6/Q7) get slower under split. Write-throughput overhead against RocksDB is 10.09% to 21.25% (Table 2): under 16% for a single transformation and about 20% for two. Secondary-index (augment) queries show gains of 'several hundred thousand times' only because plain RocksDB has to do full table scans.
hardware: 2x 16-core CPUs @ 3.00GHz, 128GB ECC RAM, two 480GB SATA SSDs, Ubuntu 20.04.6 LTS
tradeoffs: Query speedup is achieved by embedding data transformations (e.g. cross-column-family merges) into RocksDB's compaction process, which measurably reduces write throughput (16%-20% overhead) -- a direct read/write tradeoff, not a free win; benefit is workload/query-type dependent.
caveats: The headline metric is read/query latency, not throughput. The 4.25x win partly comes from a data-format change (JSON to FlatBuffers) that the baseline does not get. Row-retrieving queries are slower under the split transform, and the index-query gains compare against RocksDB full scans (not like-for-like). The CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated. The paper is an arXiv preprint with no journal-ref and says its code is 'hidden due to anonymity'. A probable anonymized review repo (github.com/anon-rev-repo/mycelium-anon, created 2026-07-27, 0 stars) describes Mycelium as a RocksDB-based LSM that piggybacks transformations on compaction and includes a YCSB harness under src/test/ycsb. The paper does not link it, it uses newer terminology (WHLSM, LSM-Grove, mRoutines), and it has no top-level license (only the vendored RocksDB licenses under src/lsm).

The record's metric field says 'throughput' but the headline is latency; metric is not a correctable field, so the orchestrator may want to fix it by hand. repo_url could plausibly be set to https://github.com/anon-rev-repo/mycelium-anon (anonymous, unlicensed), but the paper does not link it, so attribution is inferred from its name and description.

name: Nova-LSM
workload: YCSB RW50/SW50/W100 workloads (R100 also used for response times), 1 KB records, 10 GB to 2 TB databases, Uniform and Zipfian access, on 1 server and on 10 servers, with logging disabled for all systems. Nova-LSM (disaggregated LTC/StoC components over RDMA) is compared with LevelDB and RocksDB in single-instance, 64-instance and tuned-knob configurations on CloudLab APT c6220 nodes.
claimed_speedup: 2.3x to 18x higher throughput than LevelDB and RocksDB with a skewed (Zipfian) access pattern and a 2 TB database on 10 nodes (paper's contribution list), with comparable throughput under Uniform access. The 105x figure is not a distributed result. It comes from a single server with a 10 GB database on SW50 (50% scan/50% write) Zipfian, measured relative to ONE LevelDB instance (omega=1), and the paper gives 8x against LevelDB with 64 instances. The Figure 18a bar labels (LevelDB=1) put RocksDB at 6, RocksDB-tuned at 36 and RocksDB* (64 instances) at 73 against Nova-LSM's 105. That is roughly 17.5x, 2.9x and 1.4x over those RocksDB configurations (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The repo's CMakeLists.txt hard-codes /usr/bin/g++ (version unstated) with -std=c++11 -fexceptions -g, and the README build is a plain 'cmake . && make -j4' with no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE. Build flags for the LevelDB/RocksDB baselines are unstated.
hardware: CloudLab APT c6220 nodes: 64GB RAM, two 8-core Xeon E5-2650v2 CPUs (32 vCPUs w/ hyperthreading), 1TB HDD, Mellanox FDR CX3 InfiniBand (56Gbps) + 10Gbps Ethernet
tradeoffs: Disaggregates storage from compute across networked components (RDMA), which requires a multi-node RDMA cluster (InfiniBand) rather than the single-node embedded deployment RocksDB/LevelDB target; large speedups are specific to skewed multi-tenant access patterns that a disaggregated design can load-balance, not representative of typical single-node embedded use.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (SIGMOD 2021, DOI 10.1145/3448016.3457297), but the compiler version and flags are unstated, and the repo's default build adds -g without an optimization level. The 105x figure is single-node and measured against a single untuned LevelDB instance; against 64-instance RocksDB* the same scenario is only about 1.4x (derived from page data). The abstract's 'several orders of magnitude' is not borne out by the figures. With Uniform access, throughput is comparable or lower: there is a 15% range-index overhead on SW50 single-node, and the paper reports 20-30% degradation on CPU-intensive uniform workloads. On tmpfs, RocksDB* beats Nova-LSM on SW50. The system needs RDMA/InfiniBand and was evaluated on dated HDD-based nodes with logging disabled. The code is an extension of LevelDB 1.22 (its CMake project is named leveldb), although it is not a GitHub fork.
found_via: arXiv API query all:key-value+store+AND+all:outperform+AND+all:RocksDB -> arxiv.org/abs/2104.01305; code via gh search repos "Nova-LSM"

It is not A because the compiler version and flags are unstated, even though the code and experiment scripts are public (scripts/exp/nova_rocksdb_comparison.sh, nova_rocksdb_10servers.sh, plus the NovaLSM-YCSB-Client repo) and the CPU (Xeon E5-2650v2) is named. The >50x cap does not apply: against the named RocksDB baseline the reported gains are at most about 18x, and the 105x figure is against a single LevelDB instance, with an architectural explanation given.

name: ToplingDB
workload: db_bench fillrandom, fillseq and fillseq (CSPP) suites (fill, flush, compact, readseq x3, readrandom): 50,000,000 records, 8-byte keys, 50-byte values, batch_size 1000. The DB lives on /dev/shm (tmpfs) and the on-disk DB (~1.9 GiB for fillrandom) fits inside the 7.8 GiB RocksDB block cache. ToplingDB uses ToplingZipTable (zipkeyonly/zipkeyvalue), the CSPP memtable and -enable_zero_copy.
claimed_speedup: Run of 2026-09-15 (run_id 34935695406), fillrandom suite, readrandom stage. ToplingDB zipkeyvalue reached 1,735,572 ops/sec vs 348,705 for RocksDB v8.10 (4.98x, stated on the page, which calls this 'the fairest comparison') and vs 378,878 for RocksDB master (4.58x, on page). ToplingDB zipkeyonly, which stores values uncompressed while RocksDB uses Snappy/Zstd, reached 4,720,755 ops/sec: 13.54x vs v8.10 and 12.46x vs master (on page). Other stages: fillrandom 1,660,002 vs 664,354 ops/sec (2.50x, on page) and readseq 16,936,378 vs 10,771,647 (1.57x, on page). ToplingDB is slower on compaction: zipkeyvalue runs at 0.62x of v8.10 in the fillrandom suite and 0.30x in the fillseq suite. The page is a live dashboard, so the numbers change with each CI run.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated on the page. The public CI workflow builds ToplingDB with `make ... DEBUG_LEVEL=0` and upstream RocksDB with DEBUG_LEVEL=0 PORTABLE=haswell (to match ToplingDB's -march=haswell). The compiler is the ubuntu-latest default (gcc) unless the workflow's use_clang input is set, and the version is unstated.
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor (4 logical CPUs; GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner, Azure kernel 6.17), Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, 15.6 GiB RAM, DB on /dev/shm
tradeoffs: GPL-2.0 is more restrictive than RocksDB's BSD/Apache-2.0 dual license, which can block adoption in permissively-licensed downstream projects. Several advertised features (distributed compaction, some CSPP tooling) are gated behind a separate paid 'Enterprise' build not in this open repo.
caveats: The benchmark is run and published by the ToplingDB project itself, and the results page does not name the compiler. The dataset sits entirely in cache on tmpfs, which the page itself calls a CPU/memory comparison, so the result may not carry over to larger-than-cache workloads. The 13.5x headline uses zipkeyonly, which leaves values uncompressed against a compressed RocksDB and uses 1.24-1.97x more disk; the fair zipkeyvalue figure is ~5x. Compaction is slower than RocksDB. Most importantly, the components benchmarked, the ToplingZipTable builder (private topling-rocks repo) and the CSPP MemTable (private), are closed source; the build downloads them as precompiled 90-day trial objects. Only the RocksDB-derived core and some plugins are open (GPL-2.0/Apache-2.0 inherited from RocksDB).
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos --topic embedded-database --sort stars

verification.tier_reason: A first-party live CI dashboard against RocksDB v8.10.2 and RocksDB master. The code is public (.github/workflows/db_bench-build.yml, db_bench-run.yml, .github/scripts/build_upstream_rocksdb.sh, .github/bench-conf) and the page states the CPU model (AMD EPYC 7763, 4 vCPU). The workflow shows release builds (DEBUG_LEVEL=0, PORTABLE=haswell), but neither the page nor the run states which compiler or version was used; a use_clang input switches between gcc and clang. So not A.
verification.notes: The numbers match the 2026-09-15 run. The record's 'RocksDB master 378,000' should read 378,878, and the 13.5x ratio is printed on the page, not just derived. ToplingDB is a RocksDB fork (the README says 'forked from RocksDB', and db_bench reports version 8.10.2), even though GitHub's fork flag is false. The key performance components are proprietary trial binaries, hence usability 'mixed'.

workload: Binary KV operations (scan, batch read, read, read & update 1:1, read & upsert 19:1, batch upsert, remove) via the UCSB harness, UDisk vs RocksDB. The table does not give the collection size; the page links separate UCSB result posts for 1 TB and 10 TB collections.

claimed_speedup: Speedb's sorted hash memtable vs RocksDB v7.2.2 with its skiplist memtable: "Up to 155% improvement in overwrite workload", "Up to 68% improvement in 50% random read workload", "Up to 15% improvement in random seek workload". Per-point values are only in chart images. The README and dynamic-delayed-writes doc only show a chart (no numbers) of steady random-write throughput without stalls vs RocksDB's older delayed-write mechanism.
hardware: Memtable test: 16 CPU cores, model not stated. Delayed-write test in the README: 16 cores of an Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C @ 2.80GHz (per the dynamic-delayed-writes doc).
tradeoffs: 100% RocksDB-API-compatible drop-in, so switching cost for existing RocksDB users is near zero.
caveats: First-party vendor docs, and the figures are 'up to' headlines; per-point results exist only as chart images. The sorted hash memtable is opt-in (--memtablerep=speedb.HashSpdRepFactory), not the default. The baseline is old: RocksDB v7.2.2. No compiler, flags or CPU model are given for the memtable test. The README's delayed-write chart has no numbers. docs.speedb.io no longer resolves; the docs survive in the speedb-io/documentation GitHub repo. name: LIPP (Updatable Learned Index with Precise Positions)
baseline: STX B+Tree; also beats Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), ALEX, PGM-index, BwTree, and a 2-level RMI ("Learned Index")
workload: Point lookups/inserts on four datasets (Longitudes 1B, Longlat 200M, Lognormal 190M, YCSB 200M keys) under Read-Only, Read-Heavy, Write-Heavy, Write-Only workloads, single-threaded
claimed_speedup: Up to 2.8x/6.3x/15.3x/9.8x throughput vs ALEX/PGM/Learned-Index/B+Tree on read-only workloads; 2.9x/13.5x/5.4x/3.7x vs ALEX/PGM/B+Tree/ART on read-write workloads
hardware: Intel Core i7 (4 cores, 8 threads) @ 4.0GHz, 32GB RAM, Ubuntu 18.04, single thread used
tradeoffs: No concurrency support; amortized O(log^2 N) insert cost vs B+Tree's better worst case; needs periodic subtree adjustment; benefit shrinks a lot on highly non-uniform key distributions
caveats: Single-threaded benchmarks only. Gains vary strongly by dataset: as low as 1.47x vs ALEX on the highly non-uniform Longlat dataset. The paper names no CPU model (only '4.0 GHz Intel Core i7') and its benchmark harness against the baselines is not public; the repo ships only the core header and examples. The GRE study (PVLDB 15(11) 2022) found and fixed two bugs in LIPP (merged as PRs #11/#12). It reports that the fixes gave slightly lower performance than the LIPP paper reported, and that LIPP's unified node design scales poorly with multiple threads. Repo unmaintained since Feb 2022.
found_via: GitHub code search 'updatable learned index' + citation from the PGM-index/ALEX literature; verified via PVLDB paper PDF (Sections 6.1-6.2)

verification.tier_reason: The PVLDB 14(8) 2021 paper is peer-reviewed. Section 6.2 compares LIPP with STX B+Tree, ART, ALEX, PGM, Learned Index and BwTree, and it states GCC 9.0.1 at O3. It does not reach A: the CPU is given only as a '4.0 GHz Intel Core i7 (4 cores and 8 threads)' with no model number, and the comparison harness was never published (the repo holds only src/core and src/examples).
verification.notes: The numbers match Sections 6.2.1 and 6.2.2 exactly: 2.8x/6.3x/15.3x/9.8x read-only and 2.9x/13.5x/5.4x/3.7x read-write, plus the 1.47x Longlat figure. The metadata checks out: MIT, 63 stars, last commit 2022-02-07, not a fork. An independent third-party suite, GRE (github.com/gre4index/GRE, src/benchmark/microbench.cpp vs src/competitor/btree/btree.h = STX), states gcc 8.3.0 -O3 on a Xeon Platinum 8268 and shows LIPP/ALEX beating traditional indexes single-threaded. Its heatmap gives no numeric ratios, though, so I did not use it to keep tier A; enrichment could pull numbers from GRE runs.

corrected_fields.caveats: Single-threaded benchmarks only; gains vary strongly by dataset (as low as 1.47x vs ALEX on the highly non-uniform Longlat dataset); repo unmaintained since Feb 2022

name: ALEX (Adaptive Learned indEX)
baseline: STX B+Tree (std::map-like ordered index); also beats Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), a 2-stage RMI ("Learned Index"), and a Model-enhanced B+Tree
workload: Single-threaded throughput on 4 datasets with 8-byte keys: longitudes (1B keys), longlat (200M), lognormal (190M) and YCSB (200M, 80-byte payloads). Five workloads: read-only, read-heavy (95% reads/5% inserts), write-heavy (50/50), short range scans (95% scans/5% inserts) and write-only.
claimed_speedup: Up to 4.1x/2.2x/2.9x/3.0x higher throughput and 800x/15x/160x/8000x smaller index than B+Tree/Learned-Index/Model-B+Tree/ART on read-only workloads; up to 4.0x/2.7x/2.7x higher throughput and 2000x/475x/36000x smaller index vs B+Tree/Model-B+Tree/ART on read-write workloads
hardware: Intel Core i9-9900K 3.6GHz, 64GB RAM, Ubuntu Linux, single-threaded
stars_or_usage: 701 stars; used as a baseline by many follow-up learned-index papers (LIPP, CARMI, etc.)
tradeoffs: No concurrency support in the public implementation; can degrade under adversarial/skewed insert patterns without retraining; README explicitly calls it 'a near drop-in replacement for std::map'
caveats: The paper states hardware (i9-9900K, 64GB) but no compiler or optimization flags. The public repo's benchmark (src/benchmark/main.cpp) runs only ALEX, so the B+Tree/ART comparison cannot be reproduced from the repo. The baseline is STX B+Tree, not std::map. Later peer-reviewed work corroborates the win: LIPP (PVLDB'21) and GRE (PVLDB'22, gcc 8.3.0 -O3, Xeon Platinum 8268) found ALEX among the top single-threaded indexes against STX B+Tree/ART/HOT.
found_via: Starting query variation: 'in-memory learned index drop-in replacement std::map faster than B-tree'

verification.tier_reason: The peer-reviewed SIGMOD'20 paper (arXiv 1905.08898) shows ALEX beating STX B+Tree, ART, a 2-level RMI and a Model B+Tree on an Intel Core i9-9900K. It states no compiler or flags, and the repo's src/benchmark/main.cpp benchmarks ALEX alone with no baseline harness, so it cannot be A.
verification.notes: All claimed ratios appear verbatim in Section 6 (4.1x/2.2x/2.9x/3.0x read-only; 4.0x/2.7x/2.7x read-write; index-size ratios). Two fields were wrong: compared_against_cpp_std_directly was set true, but the paper benchmarks STX B+Tree, not std::map; and the workload said all datasets were 200M keys, but longitudes is 1B and lognormal 190M. The metadata checks out: MIT, 701 stars, last commit 2024-03-12 (stale), not a fork.

name: ART Synchronized (Optimistic Lock Coupling / ROWEX for Adaptive Radix Tree)
baseline: Masstree (concurrent B-tree/trie hybrid key-value index) -- not one of the assignment's named baselines, recorded honestly as the incumbent the paper actually benchmarks against
workload: Concurrent lookup, insert and remove throughput at 1-20 threads on 50M random 8-byte integer keys (low contention). A contention test runs 1 lookup thread and 1 insert+remove thread on 10M dense keys with Zipf skew. Lookup and insert run at 20 threads on three string datasets: genome (256K), Wikipedia titles (16M) and URLs (6.4M). The comparison covers the ART synchronization variants (lock coupling, Optimistic Lock Coupling, ROWEX, HTM) against Masstree.
claimed_speedup: On 50M random 8-byte integer keys, Optimistic Lock Coupling and ROWEX beat Masstree clearly (approximate values read off Figure 5, derived from page data). At 20 threads, lookups run at ~82-86M ops/s vs ~29M (~3x), inserts at ~56M vs ~24M (~2.3x), and removes at ~38M vs ~26M (~1.5x). The per-lookup cycle table gives OLC 348/418 cycles vs Masstree 982/1231 at 1/20 threads, ~2.8-2.9x fewer (derived from page data). The text says OLC needs 4.8x fewer instructions and 3.6x fewer L3 misses than Masstree. On string keys at 20 threads (Figure 7), synchronized ART beats Masstree only on genome inserts (~29M vs ~7M ops/s). Masstree is roughly on par for genome lookups and faster on both Wikipedia and URL.
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2687W v3 (Haswell EP, 10 cores/20 threads), 25MB L3 cache
tradeoffs: Requires jemalloc and TBB; ROWEX needs custom epoch-based memory reclamation and is the most complex variant to implement/maintain; the paper itself notes the ART-vs-Masstree comparison is not apples-to-apples since the synchronization protocols and data structures differ
caveats: The paper itself says ART vs Masstree is not apples-to-apples. ART's big win is on short integer keys; on string keys at 20 threads, Masstree matches or beats synchronized ART everywhere except genome inserts, including Wikipedia and URL lookups and inserts. Synchronization costs ~65% vs unsynchronized ART single-threaded, falling to ~10% at 20 threads. Compiler and flags are not stated, and no benchmark harness against Masstree is published. Masstree is not one of the assignment's named baselines. The last commit (2026-05-25, authored 2026-05-24) fixes a new-delete-type-mismatch memory-corruption bug after ~4 years of inactivity, so treat 'active' loosely.
found_via: GitHub topic search 'adaptive radix tree concurrent' -> cross-referenced against the ART synchronization DaMoN 2016 paper

verification.tier_reason: The peer-reviewed DaMoN 2016 paper benchmarks the synchronized ART variants against Masstree on a Xeon E5-2687W v3. It states no compiler or flags and publishes no comparison harness (the repo's example.cpp does not include Masstree), so B holds, but the claim was misstated.
verification.notes: The record's claim of 'roughly 2x on genome and URL' is wrong. In Figure 7, Masstree is faster on URL lookups and inserts, and genome lookups are close to a tie. The strong, supportable win is on integer keys (Figure 5 and the CPU-counter table). The LICENSE file is Apache-2.0 (gh reports NOASSERTION), stars are 129, and the repo is not a fork. GRE (PVLDB'22) independently lists ART-OLC, not Masstree, among its 24-thread winners, but I did not verify that GRE uses this repo's implementation.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: ROWEX/Optimistic Lock Coupling beat Masstree by roughly 2x on lookup/insert throughput for the genome and URL string datasets at 20 threads; Masstree is faster on the Wikipedia dataset and closes the gap with longer keys
corrected_fields.workload: Concurrent lookup/insert/remove throughput at up to 20 threads on 50M random 8-byte integer keys (low contention), plus lookup/insert at 20 threads on three string datasets (genome 256K keys, Wikipedia 16M titles, URL 6.4M URLs), comparing ART synchronization variants (Optimistic Lock Coupling, ROWEX, HTM) vs Masstree
corrected_fields.caveats: Results are mixed across datasets (Masstree wins on the Wikipedia string dataset); Masstree is not one of the assignment's named baselines; the last GitHub push (2026-05-24) is likely a housekeeping commit on an otherwise ~2015-era codebase, so treat 'active' loosely

name: Bourbon (learned index for LSM-trees, OSDI'20 artifact)
baseline: WiscKey (the authors' LevelDB-derived LSM with key-value separation; no direct stock-LevelDB or RocksDB comparison)
workload: Read-only lookups (10M operations, 16B integer keys, 64B values, in-memory) on six datasets (linear, seg-1%, seg-10%, normal with 64M keys; Amazon Reviews 33.5M; NY OpenStreetMaps 21.9M), comparing Bourbon's per-file greedy piecewise-linear-regression models (error bound 8) with the WiscKey baseline; plus YCSB, SOSD, Optane SSD and limited-memory runs.
claimed_speedup: Abstract: "BOURBON improves lookup performance by 1.23x-1.78x as compared to state-of-the-art production LSMs". In Fig. 9 the baseline is WiscKey, with 1.23x-1.78x lower average lookup latency across six datasets. vs WiscKey elsewhere: YCSB-C about 1.6x, YCSB-B/D 1.24x-1.44x, YCSB-A/F 1.06x-1.18x, YCSB-E 1.16x-1.19x; SOSD 1.48x-1.74x; Optane SSD 1.25x-1.28x; SATA SSD with limited memory 1.04x (uniform) and 1.25x (zipfian).
compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated; built with cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RELEASE -DNDEBUG_SWITCH=ON (ARTIFACT_README/CS736_README)
hardware: 20-core Intel Xeon CPU E5-2660, 160 GB memory, 480 GB SATA SSD (CloudLab c220g2 per ARTIFACT_README); the fast-storage runs used an Intel Optane SSD.
tradeoffs: Learned index is trained per SSTable file at compaction time using a cost-benefit rule to decide when learning is worthwhile; benefits are workload/data-distribution dependent (helps most when keys within a file are well-approximated by a piecewise-linear model).
caveats: The only baseline is WiscKey (a research LSM built on LevelDB), despite the abstract's 'production LSMs' wording; there is no RocksDB or stock-LevelDB head-to-head. Gains are for lookups only, with integer keys; string keys and key compression are unsupported, and writes are not improved. This GitHub repo is not the authors' own: a third party (Edward Fang) imported it as a snapshot ('original bourbon', 2020-10-11) of the authors' Bitbucket learned-leveldb artifact. It then added CS736 course-project changes (offline/synchronous level learning, 'mode 9') and a 2023 PLR NaN-slope fix. The README says the owner is not the paper's author. Compiler is unstated.
found_via: gh search repos "bourbon" (surfaced edydfang/Bourbon, 'A Learned Index for Log-Structured Merge Trees'); paper abstract opened at https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi20/presentation/dai

name: CARMI (Cache-Aware RMI)
baseline: STX B+Tree and ALEX; also beats RMI on the SOSD benchmark platform
workload: 7 datasets: 4 synthetic (lognormal, uniform, normal, exponential; 1GB each of <double,double> pairs) plus YCSB, OSMC and Facebook (67,108,864 records each). Workloads: read-only, write-heavy (50/50), read-heavy (95/5), write-partial (85% reads / 15% inserts concentrated in 60-90% of key range) and range scan, with uniform and Zipfian access; single-threaded, 100,000 operations per workload. Plus SOSD: amzn/face/wiki/osmc real-world datasets of 200M 32/64-bit keys, 10M uniform lookups.
claimed_speedup: Average 2.2x (up to 4.2x) speedup vs STX B+ Tree and 1.9x (up to 7.2x) vs ALEX, using ~0.77x the memory of the B+ Tree; on the SOSD platform the average speedup over the nearest competitor, RMI, is 1.2x (1.21x, up to 1.5x). In SOSD Table 3, ART is slightly faster on face32 (182.36 vs 187.43 ns) and RMI/RS are within ~1-5 ns on face64/wiki.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 3700X 8-core CPU, 32GB RAM, Ubuntu Linux, single-threaded
tradeoffs: Read/static-friendly cost model; construction is more expensive due to a cost-based dynamic-programming search; gains shrink on already cache-friendly small datasets
caveats: Very low adoption (10 stars) and the repo has not been updated since Jan 2022. Numbers are the authors' own, from a peer-reviewed PVLDB 2022 paper. The abstract's 'outperforms all baselines on SOSD' is slightly overstated: ART beats CARMI on face32 and RMI is effectively tied on face64. No compiler or flags are stated. The lambda parameter is tuned per dataset.
found_via: gh search repos 'cache aware learned index' -> embryo-labs/CARMI, cross-checked against the arXiv preprint (2103.00858)

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed paper (arXiv 2103.00858, published as PVLDB 15(11):2679-2691, 2022, DOI 10.14778/3551793.3551823) benchmarks CARMI against STX B+ Tree and ALEX and, on the SOSD platform, against RMI/RS/ALEX/FAST/ART/B+Tree etc. The CPU (AMD Ryzen 3700X) is stated and the code is public (embryo-labs/CARMI src/ with bundled stx_btree and alex), but no compiler or flags are given, so it cannot be A.
verification.notes: The abstract numbers match the record. The workload's '~10^8 keys' was wrong: real datasets have 67,108,864 records, and the 10^8 in the paper is a key-value multiplier for the synthetic data. GitHub metadata was verified: MIT, 10 stars, not a fork, last commit 2022-01-03, so abandoned is correct.

name: Cuckoo Trie
workload: YCSB-C (100% lookup, uniform distribution) on the osm dataset (real-world key distribution, >=1GB index, exceeding LLC capacity), single-threaded, comparing the Cuckoo Trie against STX B-Tree, ARTOLC, HOT, and Wormhole.
claimed_speedup: "the Cuckoo Trie outperforms the other indexes—by up to 35% (HOT), 20% (ARTOLC), 50% (Wormhole) and 360% (STX) on YCSB-C with osm."
compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.5.0 (paper). Cuckoo Trie: -O3 -fvisibility=hidden -flto -fno-strict-aliasing -march=haswell -DNDEBUG (Makefile). Baselines in other-benchmarked-indexes: STX and HOT -O3 -march=native, ARTOLC -O3, Wormhole driver -O2.
hardware: Dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6132 (Skylake), 14 cores @ 2.6GHz per socket, 96GB DDR4-2666 per NUMA node, hyper-threading/Turbo-Boost disabled
tradeoffs: Exploits memory-level parallelism via a cuckoo hash table layout; requires 2MB huge pages and a huge-page-aware allocator (e.g. jemalloc) to hit reported numbers, x86_64/Linux only; performs worse than other tries on keys with long common prefixes (its worst case, the 'az' dataset) and on scan-heavy workloads where its DRAM-access overlap trick doesn't help.
caveats: Research code: the README says it 'was created to run the experiments in the paper' and 'is not robust enough to be used as an index in your program'. It runs on Linux x86_64 only and needs 2MB huge pages plus a huge-page allocator (jemalloc, THP) for paper-level numbers. The Cuckoo Trie is slower on the az dataset (long common prefixes), on scan-heavy YCSB-E, and on inserts vs ARTOLC. The 360% win is over the STX B+-tree (tlx), not std::map. Optimization flags differ slightly across the compared indexes. Unlicense is a public-domain dedication with no patent grant. The baselines' benchmark repo (other-benchmarked-indexes) has no license.

name: fast64 (FAST: Fast Architecture Sensitive Tree, 64-bit)
workload: Point lookups (10M random lookup keys) on the SOSD amzn dataset (200M keys), comparing FAST against a tuned STX B-Tree. The Table 2 numbers are for a 32-bit version of amzn, which SOSD runs through this crate's create_fast32 path. The 64-bit results (Fig. 7 Pareto, Fig. 10, Fig. 16 multithreading) appear only as plots.
claimed_speedup: Table 2 (32-bit amzn, fastest variant of each structure): FAST 435.33 ns/lookup (102.0 MB) vs BTree 482.11 ns/lookup (166.0 MB), about 1.1x lower latency (derived from page data). IBTree is 446.55 ns and plain binary search 741.69 ns. Separately, FAST had the highest relative multithreaded speedup of any structure tested: 32x throughput at 40 threads against its own single-thread run.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. From the code: SOSD's CMakeLists.txt adds -ffast-math -Wall -march=native (plus -fopenmp), and fast64's c/Makefile builds the AVX-512 lookup with gcc -O3 -march=native. The compiler used for the paper runs is unstated.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPU @ 2.10GHz, 256GB RAM (20 physical / 40 logical cores for the multithreading experiment)
tradeoffs: Read-only, static tree built once; relies heavily on AVX-512 for its throughput and multithreaded scaling advantage, so results are CPU-generation dependent; build times are among the slowest of the structures SOSD tested.
caveats: The single-thread margin over STX B-Tree in Table 2 is small (about 10%), and that table uses 32-bit keys, not 64-bit. The 32x claim is a self-relative multithreading speedup, not a multithreaded FAST-vs-BTree comparison, so do not read it as a 32x win over BTree. The fast lookup path is AVX-512 C code (build.rs checks for avx512f); machines without it get a slower safe Rust path. In the same paper FAST is slower than the learned indexes (RMI 180.90 ns, RS 266.58 ns, PGM 326.48 ns) and the hash tables, and it has one of the longest build times.
found_via: Discovered via SOSD's .gitmodules (fast64 -> RyanMarcus/fast64); numbers from SOSD VLDB'21 paper Table 2 and Section 4.5 (http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol14/p1-marcus.pdf)

verification.tier_reason: The peer-reviewed PVLDB 14(1) SOSD paper (Marcus et al.) benchmarks FAST against the STX B-Tree. Table 2 gives FAST 435.33 ns / 102.0 MB against BTree 482.11 ns / 166.0 MB, and Sec. 4.5 states the 32x at 40 threads. It is not A: the benchmark code is public (learnedsystems/SOSD, benchmarks/benchmark_fast64.cc plus competitors/fast64_search.h, which wraps this repo as a submodule) and the CPU is named (Xeon Gold 6230), but neither the paper nor the SOSD README states a compiler or version.
verification.notes: Metadata checked and correct: GPL-3.0, 8 stars, last commit 2020-04-23, not a fork, not archived, so abandoned. SOSD pulls this repo in as the fast64 git submodule and uses it for both the FAST32 and FAST64 competitors, so the Table 2 FAST row does belong to this project. SOSD's older SSE competitors/fast.h is a separate class.

name: HOT (Height Optimized Trie)
workload: YCSB workload C (100% read) and workload E (95% short range-scan, 5% insert) over 50M-entry url/email/yago/integer key data sets, single node, comparing HOT against the STX B+-Tree, ART, and Masstree.
claimed_speedup: "For the lookup-only workload C, HOT achieves an at least 25% higher throughput across all evaluated data sets compared to the other evaluated index structures... In case of the URL data set, HOT's throughput is 200% higher than for the other data structures" (workload E).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.2 (stated in the paper). The paper gives no flags. The repo's CMakeLists.txt Release build (default USEAVX2=ON) uses -std=c++14 -march=native -mavx -mavx2 -mbmi2 -mlzcnt -O3 -DNDEBUG.
hardware: Intel i7-6700 (4-core, 3.4GHz/4.0GHz turbo) and Intel i9-7900X (10-core, 3.3GHz/4.3GHz turbo)
tradeoffs: Header-only, order-preserving trie with a variable per-node bit span for balance; uses the most memory-efficient layout of the four structures tested in its own paper, but ART shows 50% higher insertion throughput than HOT on pure-integer keys; string-heavy tries (Masstree, ART) grow space 51-230% on long textual keys where HOT only grows 26%.
caveats: SIGMOD 2018 peer-reviewed paper. It states two CPU models and GCC 7.2 but no optimization flags, which caps it at Tier B. The 200% (3x) margin is workload E on the url data set only; workload C is at least 25%. ART inserts 50% faster than HOT on the integer data set. Needs AVX2/BMI2. The repo has had no pushes since 2018: treat it as a frozen academic artifact, not an actively developed library.
found_via: HN Algolia query 'Height Optimized Trie HOT' -> CMU 15-721 course mirror of the SIGMOD'18 paper PDF; repo found via gh search repos 'height optimized trie HOT'

The repo's apps/benchmarks run only HOT, and the published index-microbench fork holds only the workload generator plus STX/ART wrappers, so no public harness reproduces the comparison. Not A.

name: PGM-index (Piecewise Geometric Model index)
baseline: STX B+-tree (v0.9) and cache-efficient CSS-tree (authors' implementation), plus a 2-stage RMI (Recursive Model Index)
workload: Point queries on a Web Logs dataset (~715M timestamps, 8-byte keys, 128-byte payload), 10M random queries against an in-memory sorted array index
claimed_speedup: Static: PGM-index matches the fastest STX B+-tree's query latency using ~10,000x less space (87 KiB vs 874 MiB, 'four orders of magnitude') and matches the fastest CSS-tree using 82.7x less space (4 MiB vs 341 MiB); it dominates the 2-stage RMI in the space-time trade-off (RMI MAE 892±3729 vs 226±139 for PGM; RMI built 14.5x slower). Dynamic: the Dynamic PGM-index was 13-71% faster than the STX B+-tree for most query/update mixes (1.0% and 15.2% slower at 0.8 and 0.9 query fractions), using 611-3891x less space.
hardware: 2.3 GHz Intel Xeon Gold CPU, 192 GiB memory
stars_or_usage: 874 stars; basis for the PyGM Python wrapper, widely cited in follow-on learned-index papers
tradeoffs: Base structure targets static/append-friendly data (a dynamic variant exists but adds complexity); requires a sorted key array; the headline win vs traditional trees is space at matched latency, not a raw query-latency multiplier
caveats: The VLDB'20 paper states only '2.3 GHz Intel Xeon Gold' (no model), with no compiler or flags. The static comparisons against the B+-tree and CSS-tree are same-speed at far less space rather than strictly faster. The strictly-faster wins are against RMI and, in the dynamic setting, 13-71% over the STX B+-tree on most (not all) workload mixes. All numbers come from the authors' own experiments.
found_via: GitHub topic search 'learned index' + citation chain from the LIPP and CARMI papers

The CPU is only '2.3 GHz Intel Xeon Gold' (no model) and no compiler or flags are given, so it cannot be A.

name: PLEX / TrieSpline
workload: Four 64-bit SOSD real-world datasets (amzn, face, osm, wiki; 200M keys each). Build time vs size is compared against RMI, CHT, PGM and RadixSpline (Fig. 2). Lookup time vs size is compared against those plus ART and BTree (Fig. 3).
claimed_speedup: Graph-only. In Fig. 3 (size vs lookup time, 200M 64-bit keys) the PLEX curve lies at roughly 200-300 ns against BTree's roughly 500-900 ns and ART's roughly 400-600 ns on amzn and face (approximate, read from the plot). The text gives no ratio. It says 'PGM, ART, and BTree eventually lose performance as the index size is increased', and it notes that PLEX fixes RadixSpline's outlier problem on face and sits at a constant offset of about 25 ns from RMI on amzn and face. In the plot, RMI is the faster of the two.
hardware: AWS m5zn.metal instance, 48 vCPUs at 4.5GHz turbo, 192GiB RAM
tradeoffs: Single hyperparameter (max prediction error) with an auto-tuner, unlike RMI/CHT/RS which need offline grid search; read-only (no update support, follow-up work planned a Fenwick-tree extension that was not implemented in this repo).
caveats: AIDB@VLDB 2021 workshop extended abstract, not a full research-track paper. The hardware is an AWS instance type with no CPU model, and the compiler and flags are not stated. The speedup evidence is only plots with no quoted number. PLEX does not beat RMI on lookup latency (RMI is about 25 ns faster on amzn and face).
found_via: Discovered via SOSD's .gitmodules (competitors/ts -> stoianmihail/TrieSpline, GitHub-renamed to stoianmihail/PLEX); paper opened at https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.05117

verification.tier_reason: The AIDB@VLDB'21 extended abstract (peer-reviewed workshop) plots PLEX against BTree, ART, PGM, RMI, RS and CHT on the four 64-bit SOSD datasets (Fig. 3). The PLEX lookup-time curve sits well below BTree's on every dataset. It is not A: the text gives only the machine type (AWS m5zn.metal, 4.5 GHz turbo), not a CPU model, compiler or flags, and the repo's own bench_end_to_end.cc compares only against RadixSpline.

TrieSpline also ships as a SOSD competitor (competitors/ts), which is presumably how Fig. 3's BTree/ART comparison was run. Plot values above are approximate visual readings, not printed numbers.

name: RadixSpline
workload: Point lookups (10M random lookup keys) on the SOSD amzn (books) dataset of 200M keys. Table 2 specifically uses a 32-bit version of amzn and reports the best-performing (often largest) variant of each index structure, comparing RadixSpline (RS) against the STX B+ Tree, IBTree, FAST, binary search, PGM, RMI, CuckooMap and RobinHash. The Pareto plots (Fig. 7) cover 64-bit keys over amzn/face/osm/wiki.
claimed_speedup: 266.58 ns/lookup (4.0 MB) for RS vs 482.11 ns/lookup (166.0 MB) for BTree (STX B+ Tree) on the 32-bit version of the amzn dataset, fastest variant of each -> ~1.8x lower latency at ~41x less space (derived from page data, Table 2)
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The SOSD repo build (scripts/prepare.sh, CMakeLists.txt) uses CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, C++17, -ffast-math -march=native, and -fopenmp if available. The compiler is not pinned; the README installs clang on Ubuntu 20.04.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPU @ 2.10GHz, 256GB RAM
tradeoffs: Read-only, single-pass build; can be built as a drop-in replacement for std::multimap over sorted data. Degrades badly on data with a small number of extreme outliers (e.g. the 'face' dataset in SOSD), where its radix table becomes nearly useless.
caveats: Same SOSD/VLDB'21 paper as the RMI entry. The CPU is stated and the SOSD harness is public, but no compiler is named (flags only in the SOSD CMake build), so it is capped at Tier B. Table 2 numbers are for a 32-bit version of amzn and are the fastest variant per structure. RS beats PGM (326.48 ns) but trails RMI (180.90 ns), and both hash tables (CuckooMap 114.50 ns, RobinHash 93.69 ns) beat every ordered index at far larger size. RS and RBS degrade badly on the face dataset because of outliers. It is a header-only C++ library whose last commit on master is 2021-05-13 (the 2023-04-28 date is only the repo pushed_at). The SOSD harness itself is GPL-3.0, while the RS library is MIT.

name: RMI (Recursive Model Index, reference implementation)
workload: Point lookups (10M random lookup keys) on the SOSD amzn (books) dataset of 200M keys. Table 2 specifically uses a 32-bit version of amzn and reports the best-performing (often largest) variant of each index structure, comparing a CDFShop-tuned RMI against the STX B+ Tree, IBTree, FAST, binary search, PGM, RadixSpline, CuckooMap and RobinHash. The Pareto plots (Fig. 7) cover 64-bit keys over amzn/face/osm/wiki.
claimed_speedup: 180.90 ns/lookup (48.0 MB) for RMI vs 482.11 ns/lookup (166.0 MB) for BTree (STX B+ Tree) on the 32-bit version of the amzn dataset, fastest variant of each -> ~2.7x lower latency at ~3.5x less space (derived from page data, Table 2)
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The SOSD repo build (scripts/prepare.sh, CMakeLists.txt) uses CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, C++17, -ffast-math -march=native, and -fopenmp if available; the RMI code is generated by the Rust compiler (cargo). The C++ compiler is not pinned; the README installs clang on Ubuntu 20.04.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPU @ 2.10GHz, 256GB RAM
tradeoffs: Read-only: RMI requires offline training and does not support inserts without a full retrain; must be tuned (branching factor, layer types) per dataset via the CDFShop optimizer; RMI build times are slower than PGM/RadixSpline per the same paper.
caveats: The SOSD/VLDB'21 'Benchmarking Learned Indexes' paper states the CPU model and methodology, and the SOSD harness is public, but no compiler is named, so it is capped at Tier B. Table 2 numbers are for a 32-bit version of amzn and are the fastest (48 MB) RMI variant. Both hash tables (CuckooMap 114.50 ns / 1541 MB, RobinHash 93.69 ns / 6144 MB) are faster for point lookups. RMIs are read-only, need offline training, and take much longer to build than PGM/RS or B-Trees (Section 4.6). The RMI 'library' is a Rust compiler that emits C/C++ source files, and those generated files are what gets linked and benchmarked. The SOSD harness is GPL-3.0, while the RMI repo is MIT.

name: Adaptive Radix Tree (rafaelkallis/adaptive-radix-tree)
baseline: std::map (red-black tree, libstdc++) -- the closest stdlib ordered-index analog to the assignment's B-tree baseline
workload: 1.6M operations per benchmark (picobench Dim=1,600,000) with sparse keys: random mt19937_64 64-bit values formatted as decimal strings via std::to_string. Covers delete, insert, mixed, query uniform, query uniform (base-64 keys) and query Zipf, comparing art::art vs std::map<std::string,...> vs std::unordered_map<std::string,...>.
claimed_speedup: ~1.5x-2.4x faster than std::map: delete 1.985x, insert 2.118x, mixed 1.824x, query-uniform 1.517x, query-uniform base-64 keys 2.390x, query-zipf 1.817x. Against std::unordered_map, ART is slower on delete (0.691), query-uniform (0.518), query-uniform base-64 (0.655) and mixed (0.928), and at parity on insert (1.029) and query-zipf (1.005).
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build: -O3 -DNDEBUG -Wall -Wextra -fsigned-char (compiler not stated)
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0 (copyleft) limits use in permissively-licensed or proprietary code; slower than std::unordered_map for pure lookups/deletes in this benchmark; only sparse-key workload shown
caveats: First-party micro-benchmark (picobench harness, not nanobench). No compiler, stdlib or CPU is stated, and the numbers were added to the README in 2018. The README heading says '16M keys' but the table shows 1.6M. Keys are std::to_string'd random 64-bit ints, so the baseline is std::map<std::string>, and to_string cost sits inside every timed loop. The hashmap benchmark uses a random_device seed while ART and std::map use a fixed seed. GPL-3.0 license.

name: libmdbx
workload: In-tmpfs CRUD benchmarks (engine speed without disk I/O) run with the ioArena harness via 'make bench-quartet', which also covers RocksDB and WiredTiger. No dataset size, key/value sizes, hardware, or result tables are published.

In-tmpfs benchmarks that test the engine itself show libmdbx 10-20% faster than LMDB, and up to 30% faster when built with options that downgrade several runtime checks to match LMDB. The README says libmdbx may be slower than LMDB on Windows (LockFileEx locking). A separate comparison bullet asserts 'up to 10-100K times faster than both BoltDB and LMDB in particular extreme cases' (excluding disk I/O), with no data behind it.
