tradeoffs: Slower than LMDB on Windows due to native file locking; larger feature surface than LMDB increases complexity; the canonical project has moved off GitHub and this is now a mirror/transfer
caveats: Self-reported percentages with no published result tables, hardware, or compiler/flags. The ioArena harness is public (sourcecraft.dev/dqdkfa/ioarena, originally github.com/pmwkaa/ioarena). The README says libmdbx may be slower than LMDB on Windows (LockFileEx) and slower on macOS with the default F_FULLFSYNC durability setting. hardware: AWS: 4x m5n.8xlarge clients (128GB RAM, 32 vCPU, 25Gbps); brokers: i3en.large / is4gen.medium (small, 50MB/s), i3en.3xlarge (medium, 500MB/s), i3en.6xlarge (large, 1GB/s); 3 Redpanda nodes in all tiers vs 3/4/6 Kafka nodes; CPU model not stated

The modified OpenMessaging Benchmark fork is public (github.com/redpanda-data/openmessaging-benchmark; the page links its PR #37), but compiler/JVM flags and CPU models are not stated. Independent rebuttal: Jack Vanlightly (Confluent), 'Kafka vs Redpanda Performance - Do the claims add up?' (2023-05-15), re-ran it with his own OMB fork (github.com/Vanlightly/openmessaging-benchmark-custom) on 3x i3en.6xlarge. He found Kafka misconfigured (log.flush.interval.messages=1 forcing fsync per batch, Java 11), could not get Redpanda to 1000 MB/s with TLS, and saw Redpanda degrade with 50 producers (end-to-end latency up to ~24 s), after ~12 h sustained load (p99.99 ~26 s), with record keys (capped ~330 MB/s vs Kafka 500 MB/s) and at retention limits. He concludes the claims are 'greatly exaggerated'. Treat the 70x as a vendor claim.

name: Prefix Filter
workload: Space usage, false-positive rate, operation throughput at varying load, and build time for 0.94*2^28 (~252M) random 64-bit keys at false-positive rate ~2^-8, single-threaded, on an Intel Ice Lake server (PVLDB 15(7), 2022)
claimed_speedup: Build time for n=0.94*2^28 (~252M) keys: the prefix filter is faster than every cuckoo filter configuration by more than 3.2x (abstract: 3.2-3.5x) and faster than the vector quotient filter (TwoChoicer) by 1.39-1.46x. Cuckoo filter insertions slow down more than 27x as load grows, so its build time is close to that of a plain Bloom filter BF-16[k=11]. Negative-query throughput is higher than CF-12 at every load up to 95% (+55%, +40% and +2.8% at 50%, 70% and 90% load). Positive queries at 100% load are 28-40% slower than CF-12-Flex and 46-60% slower than CF-12. The plain Bloom filter is the slowest filter for queries. The blocked Bloom filter is about 2x faster than the prefix filter for all operations, but its false-positive rate is 3-6x higher. Space is 11.55-12.13 bits/key at a 0.37-0.39% false-positive rate (Table 3).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 10.3.0 on Ubuntu 20.04 (paper Sec. 7.1). The artifact repo's CMakeLists.txt builds the benchmark targets measure_perf, measure_built and measure_fpp with -Ofast -DNDEBUG, and CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS is -march=native.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6336Y (Ice Lake) @ 2.40GHz, 64GiB RAM, 48KiB L1d/1.25MiB L2 per core, 36MiB shared L3
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 hardware for the fast path; is an incremental filter (supports insertion but the paper focuses on a fixed configured capacity); this is a mixed win, not a strict speed win across every metric.
caveats: The paper's 52%/79% figure is the cuckoo filter's query-throughput lead over the vector quotient filter at high load. It is not a lead over the prefix filter, so the earlier record misattributed it. The prefix filter beats CF-12 on negative queries at every load up to 95%, but it trails cuckoo filters on positive queries at full load (by 28-60%). The blocked Bloom filter is about 2x faster than the prefix filter for all operations, at a much higher space and false-positive cost. The README requires an Intel CPU with AVX-512. All numbers come from single-threaded runs on one Ice Lake machine. The license is Apache-2.0 per LICENSE.md, although GitHub's detector reports NOASSERTION. The paper is PVLDB 15(7) 2022 (the arXiv version is the full version). There have been no commits since 2022-09-12.

name: Xor Filter (xor_singleheader)
workload: Single-threaded membership-query time against space overhead for 10M and 100M random 64-bit keys, with 25% of queried keys present (fastfilter_cpp benchmarks/bulk-insert-and-query.cc). The binary fuse paper adds construction time per key and bits/key across set sizes up to 100M keys.
claimed_speedup: This record covers both filters in FastFilter/xor_singleheader. (1) Xor filters, JEA 2020 (arXiv 1912.08258, Table 3, 25% of queried keys present): at 10M keys, Xor8 takes 23 ns/query at 9.8 bits/key, against Bloom12 at 40 ns (12.0 bits/key) and Cuckoo12 at 31 ns (12.8 bits/key). Xor16 takes 27 ns (19.7 bits/key), against Bloom16 at 48 ns (16.0 bits/key) and Cuckoo16 at 32 ns (17.0 bits/key). At 100M keys, Xor8 takes 32 ns, against Bloom12 at 58 ns and Cuckoo12 at 38 ns. (2) Binary fuse filters, JEA 2022 (arXiv 2201.01174): the 3-wise filter reaches about 9 bits/key (12.5% above the lower bound) and the 4-wise filter about 8.6 bits/key (7.5% above). Xor uses 9.84 bits/key (23% above) and Bloom at least 44% above. Construction is more than 2x faster than xor filters, and xor and cuckoo construction are both slower. The 3-wise query speed is on par with xor and faster than Bloom filters. The 4-wise query speed is similar to cuckoo filters. The binary fuse figures come only from plots; the paper has no table.
compiler_and_flags: Xor paper: GNU GCC 8.1.0, -O3 -march=native, 64-bit Linux executable. Binary fuse paper: GCC 10, -O3, plus -march=native on x64.
hardware: Intel i7-6700 @ 3.4GHz (Skylake) with 8MiB L3, the primary platform in both papers. The binary fuse paper also uses a secondary AMD EPYC 7262 (Zen 2), which has a 25% error margin.
stars_or_usage: 432 stars; used in production by Databend, ntop nDPI, InfiniFlow, and CockroachDB Pebble
tradeoffs: Immutable once built (no add/remove; must know the full key set upfront); needs a strong ~64-bit hash of the input keys; construction is slower than Bloom/blocked-Bloom (~110-130ns/key vs ~10-40ns/key at 10M keys per Table 2 of the same paper); naturally compressible with gzip/zstd, unlike Bloom/cuckoo.
caveats: This record covers both xor filters and binary fuse filters. The repo ships xorfilter.h and binaryfusefilter.h, and the README recommends binary fuse, which is smaller and faster to build than xor. Xor filter is itself a listed baseline in this category, so this entry's claim is measured against Bloom and cuckoo filters. The blocked Bloom filter is faster for queries (16 ns against Xor8's 23 ns at 10M keys) at 10.7 bits/key and about 0.94% false-positive probability. The 2020 paper found xor construction roughly half as fast as Bloom and cuckoo construction, and binary fuse removes most of that cost. The filters are static: no inserts after construction. The paper numbers were measured on the C++ implementations in fastfilter_cpp release 1.0, not on this C header, although the current harness can run the single-header code. All runs are single-threaded on one 2015-era Skylake CPU. The sample query-benchmark output in the README (98.765 ns/q, 0.123456 s) looks like placeholder text, not a measurement.

name: Adaptive Learned Bloom Filter (Ada-BF)
workload: False-positive rate vs. memory budget on a malicious-URL dataset (485,730 URLs, 16.47% malicious) and other real-world datasets; standard Bloom filter vs. learned Bloom filter (LBF), sandwiched LBF, Ada-BF, and disjoint Ada-BF
claimed_speedup: Paper: Ada-BF/disjoint Ada-BF 'reduce the FPR by over 80% and save 50% of the memory usage over existing learned Bloom filters'. On malicious URLs at a 500Kb filter size, Ada-BF cuts FPR by 81% vs LBF/sandwiched LBF (disjoint Ada-BF: 84%); at FPR ~0.35% the memory drops from over 500Kb (LBF) to 300Kb (over 40% savings). On malware MD5, 0.2% FPR needs ~300Kb for LBF vs 150Kb for Ada-BF (50%), and all learned BFs cut FPR by over 98% vs the standard Bloom filter.
tradeoffs: Requires training/maintaining a classifier model alongside the filter; memory savings depend on how well the model's score distribution separates keys from non-keys, so gains are dataset-dependent
caveats: Reference Python research code with no LICENSE file (reference/study-only). Peer-reviewed at NeurIPS 2020 as 'Adaptive Learned Bloom Filter (Ada-BF): Efficient Utilization of the Classifier with Application to Real-Time Information Filtering on the Web'. This is a numerical FPR-vs-memory comparison, not a speed benchmark: most headline gains are vs other learned Bloom filters, and the standard BF's bit budget is credited with the classifier size (146Kb on URLs). No CPU/compiler details apply. The repo also ships a PLBF.py baseline.

name: BuRR (Ribbon Filter)
workload: Space overhead, construction time and positive/negative query time (ns/key). Sequential runs use n=10^6 and 10^8 keys, and a parallel run queries 1280 filters of 10^7 keys from 64 threads. False-positive rates are about 1%, 10% and 0.05%. BuRR is compared against Bloom, blocked Bloom, cuckoo, Morton, quotient, xor, xor+ and fuse filters in the lorenzhs/fastfilter_cpp harness (SEA 2022 best paper; the arXiv version is the extended one).
claimed_speedup: Space overhead over the information-theoretic minimum (arXiv 2109.01892 Table 2, false-positive rate about 1%, r=7/8): Xor 23.0%, Xor+ 14.4%, blocked Bloom 45-52% and Cuckoo12 40-46%. Plain Bloom is at least 44% by construction (1.44*log2(1/f)). BuRR ranges from 0.06% to 1.4% depending on ribbon width (0.21-0.48% at w=64). Speed: in the 64-thread parallel workload, BuRR and homogeneous ribbon Pareto-dominate plain Bloom filters. In that workload, BuRR 2-bit w=64 takes 215/215 ns for positive/negative queries and 190 ns/key to construct, against Xor r=8 at 386/392 ns and 586 ns/key. Sequentially, the faster BuRR variants are 'only moderately slower than Bloom and Xor filters'. For example, at n=10^8, BuRR 2-bit w=64 takes 82/74 ns for positive/negative queries against Xor's 41/41 ns, and constructs at 115 against 159 ns/key. The README's rounded figures are overheads 'as low as 0.1%' and below 0.5% for speed-oriented configurations.

name: Cuckoo Filter (efficient/cuckoofilter)
workload: 192MB filters holding ~120-128M pre-generated 64-bit random-integer keys; lookup throughput measured while varying the fraction of positive queries, and insert throughput measured across load factor, on a two-socket Intel Xeon testbed.
claimed_speedup: Lookup throughput (Fig. 5, read from the plot): CF is ~12 MOPS at 0% and 100% positive queries and dips to ~10.5 MOPS at 50%. The standard Bloom filter falls from ~8.3 MOPS (0% positive) to ~4.9 MOPS (100% positive), so the CF advantage runs from ~1.45x to ~2.4x (derived from page data, plot-read). Construction is 5.00M keys/sec (CF) vs 3.91M keys/sec (BF) with all filters at 192MB, at 12.60 vs 13.00 bits/item and the same 0.19% FPR (Table 3; ~1.28x, derived from page data). On space, semi-sorted cuckoo filters need fewer bits/item than space-optimized Bloom filters when the target FPR is below 3% (crossover 7.2 bits/item, Fig. 4 and Sec. 6).
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon L5640 @ 2.27GHz, 12MB L3 cache, 32GB DRAM
tradeoffs: Supports deletion unlike standard Bloom filters, but load factor caps insert capacity (~95% full before insert failures); asymptotically worse in bits/item (O(log n)) than Bloom's O(1), though practically better for realistic table sizes with reasonably sized buckets; duplicate-heavy workloads (same item inserted >2b times) can fail insertion.
caveats: Peer-reviewed ACM CoNEXT'14 paper (Fan, Andersen, Kaminsky, Mitzenmacher). It states the hardware (2x Xeon L5640) but not the compiler or flags. The repo's benchmarks/conext-figure5.cc and conext-table3.cc only benchmark CuckooFilter, so the Bloom-filter baseline code is not public. The current benchmarks/Makefile flags (-O3 -march=core-avx2) postdate the paper and could not have run on the Westmere testbed. The CF only ties the paper's blocked Bloom filter at 0% positive queries (~12 MOPS each); its win is over the standard Bloom filter and grows with the positive-query fraction. Per Sec. 6, the <3% FPR space advantage is stated for the semi-sorting variant. The README has no numbers. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the Apache-2.0 text. Independent check: the Xor Filters paper (ACM JEA 2020, arXiv 1912.08258; i7-6700, GCC 8.1.0, -O3 -march=native) measures a modified Cuckoo 12 at 31 ns/query vs Bloom 12 at 40 ns (10M keys, 25% find). In the same paper the original implementation measures 30 ns at 20.1 bits/key (Table 4).

name: Morton Filter
workload: Fan et al.'s reference cuckoo filter (plus semi-sorted CF and RSQF) vs a Morton filter with 128*1024*1024 slots and 8-bit fingerprints (3-slot buckets). The filters are filled to each load factor in steps of 0.05. Then 0.1% of total slots are inserted, deleted or looked up with 64-bit random keys. Results are the average of 5 trials (VLDB 2018 paper).
claimed_speedup: Paper vs Fan et al.'s reference cuckoo filter (CF): lookups 1.3x-2.5x faster (1.3x-2.5x for true negatives, Fig. 11; 1.6x-2.4x for true positives, Fig. 10), insertions 0.9x-15.5x (Fig. 12), deletions 1.3x-1.6x (Fig. 13). The README's 'up to 15.5x, 1.3x, and 2.5x' understates deletion; the paper says up to 1.6x. The MF uses about 11.71 bits/item at 0.95 load vs a 12-bit-fingerprint CF. The paper does not benchmark Bloom filters. Its point about using fewer bits than a Bloom filter below ~1-3% FPR is a general statement about cuckoo/quotient filters.
compiler_and_flags: g++ 5.4.0-6 with -Ofast -march=native (paper Sec. 6). The repo benchmarking/Makefile uses -Ofast -march=native -mpopcnt -std=c++11. The README recommends g++ 5.4 and reports a GCC 8.x performance regression as of March 2019.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 1950X (2x8 cores, 32 MB L3), frequency fixed at 3400 MHz, 128 GB DDR4-2133, Ubuntu 16.04.4 LTS (Linux 4.11.0)
stars_or_usage: 90 stars; developed at AMD Research, published at VLDB 2018 with an extended version in the VLDB Journal (2019)
tradeoffs: Supports self-resizing (grow capacity without a backing structure) unlike vanilla cuckoo filters; requires only a multiple-of-two bucket count rather than a power of two; author explicitly labels the code 'academic-style prototype', not hardened for production.
caveats: The README says this is an academic prototype. The batch API works correctly only when the input is a multiple of 128. A later deletion correctness fix cut peak deletion throughput from about 38 to about 28 MOPS, so current code may not reproduce the paper's deletion numbers. Insertion speedup is 0.9x (slower) at some load factors. The repo has no commits since 2020-12-16.

name: Partitioned Learned Bloom Filter (PLBF)
workload: False-positive rate vs. space tradeoff on a synthetic dataset, a URL dataset, and the EMBER malware dataset, comparing PLBF against a theoretically-optimal Bloom filter, sandwiched learned Bloom filter, and Ada-BF
claimed_speedup: at matched space (400Kb/500Kb/3000Kb for synthetic/URLs/EMBER), PLBF achieves 22x, 26x, and 3x smaller false-positive rates than the sandwiching approach, and 8.5x, 9x, 1.9x smaller than Ada-BF; to hit FPR=0.001, sandwiching needs 8.8x/3.3x/1.2x the space of PLBF and Ada-BF needs 6x/2.5x/1.1x the space
tradeoffs: Needs a trained scoring model plus a dynamic-program solve for optimal partition thresholds; benefit shrinks when the model is weak (EMBER dataset shows only a slight improvement)
caveats: Peer-reviewed at ICLR 2021. The repo README says 'ICLR 2020', which is wrong; the CLBF paper cites it as ICLR 2021. The repo has only plbf_algo.py (threshold/FPR optimizer) and a README. It has no LICENSE file (reference/study only) and no experiment or benchmark code. The headline multipliers are against learned variants (sandwiched LBF, Ada-BF), not a raw Bloom filter. The 'optimal Bloom filter' curve is analytical (standard Bloom filter space / log2 e), and the standard-Bloom-filter comparison (Appendix E.1, Fig. 4) is shown only as a plot. The model is an sklearn random forest, sized by its pickle file. Last commit was in 2022-06, more than 3 years ago.

name: SIMD Blocked Bloom Filter (src/simd-block.h, Impala-derived)
workload: Single-threaded bulk construction and membership tests on 10M and 100M pseudo-random 64-bit keys (Murmur-finalizer hash), with 25% of queries on existing keys. Blocked Bloom (10.7 bits/key) is compared with standard Bloom filters at 8, 12 and 16 bits/key, using FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp benchmarks/bulk-insert-and-query.cc.
claimed_speedup: Xor Filters paper (Graf & Lemire, ACM JEA 2020), testing the Impala AVX2 blocked Bloom that is also used in efficient/cuckoofilter, modified for flexible sizes. Membership tests take 16 ns/query vs 31 ns (Bloom 8) and 40 ns (Bloom 12) at 10M keys with 25% find, and 20 ns vs 53 ns and 58 ns at 100M keys (Table 3; ~1.9-2.9x, derived from page data). Construction takes 10 ns/key vs 40 and 60 ns/key at 10M keys, and 20 ns/key vs 70 and 90 ns/key at 100M keys (Table 2). The trade-off is 10.7 bits/key at 0.94% FPP vs 0.31% for Bloom 12.
compiler_and_flags: GNU GCC 8.1.0, -O3 -march=native (per paper)
hardware: Intel i7-6700 (Skylake) @ 3.4 GHz, 8 MB L3
tradeoffs: Higher false positive rate than standard Bloom at equal space (0.43% vs 0.19% at 13 bits/item, Table 3) because hashing items to one of many small per-block filters creates imbalanced "hot"/"cold" blocks even with strong hash functions; no deletion support.
caveats: The original record wrongly attributed the CoNEXT'14 paper's blk-BF numbers (Table 3's 7.64M keys/sec, the Fig. 5 '~4 MOPS' gap) to this code. The paper's blocked Bloom is its own 2014 implementation with 64-byte blocks and k=9. src/simd-block.h was added to efficient/cuckoofilter by Jim Apple in Dec 2016, two years later. This repo's own benchmarks/bulk-insert-and-query.cc header shows SimdBlock8 at ~55-75M adds/sec and ~58-75M finds/sec, vs Cuckoo12 at ~16-24M adds/sec and ~32-37M finds/sec. It includes no standard Bloom and no hardware (first-party, Tier C on its own). The peer-reviewed numbers come from a modified copy in FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp src/bloom/simd-block.h, credited there as 'from apache/impala (via the cuckoo filter)'. The filter needs AVX2 (x86-only) and has a higher FPR per bit than a standard Bloom filter.

name: SuRF (Succinct Range Filter)
workload: RocksDB replacement of its Bloom filters with SuRF on a synthetic 100GB time-series dataset (2K simulated sensors, 128-bit keys); end-to-end open-range, closed-range, and worst-case (all-missing-key) point query throughput, SIGMOD 2018 Best Paper
claimed_speedup: RocksDB with SuRF vs RocksDB's Bloom filter at equal filter size: open-range (Open-Seek) queries 1.5x faster, and closed-range queries up to 5x faster (SuRF-Real, when 99% of queries return empty). On the worst-case all-miss point-query workload, the abstract says RocksDB is up to 40% slower with SuRF because of a higher false-positive rate (0.2% vs 0.1%). Fig. 12 point throughput is 32.9 Kops/s for Bloom, 19.8 for SuRF-Hash and 16.4 for SuRF-Real. So SuRF-Real is about 50% slower (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The SuRF repo's CMake Release flags are -O3 -Wall -Werror -mpopcnt -pthread -std=c++11, with the compiler unspecified. The RocksDB end-to-end runs used the efficient/rocksdb fork, whose build flags were not checked.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6770HQ CPU, 32GB RAM, Intel 540s 480GB SSD
stars_or_usage: 554 stars; SIGMOD 2018 Best Paper; evaluated as a RocksDB Bloom-filter replacement
tradeoffs: SuRF trades a higher false-positive rate for the ability to answer range queries and approximate range counts, which plain Bloom filters cannot do at all; for pure point-query, moderate-FPP workloads the paper itself says 'the Bloom filter is usually a better choice than SuRF'; construction speed is comparable to Bloom filter's.
caveats: This is a mixed result, not a strict win. SuRF is 40-50% slower for all-miss point queries at equal filter size, and the paper says adding a few suffix bits per key closes the gap. Its wins (1.5x-5x) are for range queries only. The paper reports throughput in Kops/s, not latency. The end-to-end code lives in the efficient/rocksdb fork (last push 2018-12-20). The microbenchmarks (bench/workload.cpp vs bench/filter_bloom.hpp) ran on a Xeon E5-2680 v2. The GitHub license API says NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the plain Apache-2.0 text. bench/bloom.hpp is LevelDB-derived code under a BSD-style license.

name: Vacuum Filter
workload: Positive/mixed lookup, insertion, and deletion throughput plus bits-per-item vs. target false-positive rate, 64-bit random keys, varying table occupancy 0-100%, on a DELL workstation (PVLDB 13, 2020)
claimed_speedup: Abstract: about 25% less space on average and similar throughput vs cuckoo filters, and about 15% less space and >10x throughput vs Bloom filters, at the same false-positive rate. In memory: VF-ss is about 1.1x-1.8x faster than CF-ss for positive lookups. VFs have the highest lookup throughput below 90% occupancy, but CFs are slightly better at high occupancy. VFs have the highest insertion throughput below 65% occupancy, and deletion throughput is similar to CFs. On SSD with a 100 MB memory limit, VF lookups are 1.86x-2.13x faster than CF. Space: VFs save 2-5 bits per item vs the other methods in the average case (about 5 fewer bits vs CFs).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The repo makefile builds the test.cpp demo with g++ -Ofast -march=native -mpopcnt -std=c++14 (plus -pg -g).
hardware: DELL workstation, Intel Xeon E5-2687W @ 3.00GHz, 30MB L3 cache, SK-hynix SC311-S 1TB SSD
tradeoffs: Built on top of / modified from Fan et al.'s cuckoo filter code; the fast implementation is a modified cuckoo filter rather than a from-scratch design; deletion throughput is only 'similar to' cuckoo filter, not better; insertion advantage narrows and eventually loses to cuckoo/vacuum crossover above ~65% occupancy where both slow down comparably.
caveats: The paper gives the CPU but no compiler or flags. The repo has no harness for the Bloom, Morton and CQF comparisons, only the test.cpp demo and Fan et al.'s inherited CF benchmarks under ModifiedCuckooFilter/. name: Cascaded Learned Bloom Filter (CLBF)
workload: Memory-vs-FPR (target F from 0.1 to 0.001) and memory-vs-reject-time trade-offs on the URL, Ember and Higgs datasets (14 datasets in the appendix), using XGBoost models and 10,000 held-out test non-keys. Baselines are all in C++: classical Bloom filter (fastfilter_cpp), PLBF (via Fast PLBF), Sandwiched LBF, G-PLBF, Ensemble LBF, PHBF and HABF.
claimed_speedup: At the same FPR, CLBF uses up to 17% less memory than the best PLBF configuration, for example on Ember at F=0.005. It cuts reject time by up to 14.6x vs PLBF under the default XGBoost setting, and by up to 65x across the appendix model variants. Construction takes 1.003x-1.23x longer than existing LBFs. A classical Bloom filter (fastfilter_cpp) is plotted as a baseline in Fig. 5, but no CLBF-vs-Bloom ratio is quoted. PLBF is described as the most memory-efficient LBF under a fixed model; G-PLBF matches CLBF on memory vs FPR.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.4.0 with -O3, single-threaded (paper Section 6); repo builds with CMake Release inside an Ubuntu 22.04 Docker image
hardware: Linux, Intel Core i9-11900H @ 2.50 GHz, 64 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Adds a DP-based size/threshold optimizer at construction time (paper reports this is 0.3-24% of total build time); like other learned filters, needs a trained scoring model and benefits are dataset/model dependent
caveats: The record said there was no code, but that was wrong. The official implementation is https://github.com/atsukisato/CascadedLBF (Apache-2.0, C++, Docker-based reproduction scripts for CLBF and all baselines, 0 stars, created 2026-01). The repo_url should be set to it, but that field cannot be corrected here. The paper itself does not link the repo. The headline memory figure is against PLBF, not a classical Bloom filter. Reject time includes ML inference, so a plain Bloom filter may still reject faster. The source is arXiv v2 (2026-08-24), and no peer-review venue was confirmed.

name: ChainedFilter
workload: RocksDB (all SSTables in L0, default 64MB write buffer, 36-byte random keys and 64-byte values, 4M-16M items) P70/P99 point-query latency with ChainedFilter replacing the built-in Bloom filter, versus Bloom-only filters at 0x/1x/2x space; also external-memory accesses for Cuckoo Hashing, static-dictionary space and Learned Bloom Filter space
claimed_speedup: SIGMOD 2024 paper: up to 36% lower P99 tail point-query latency than RocksDB's built-in Bloom filter at the same filter space (|U|=16M existing-item queries: about 31us for Bloom vs under 20us for ChainedFilter); up to 31% fewer external memory accesses than raw Cuckoo Hashing; 26% extra space over the theoretical lower bound for an implicit static dictionary; 0.22 extra bits/item over the lower bound for lossless compression; up to 99.1% less filter space than the original Learned Bloom Filter
compiler_and_flags: g++ 7.5.0 (Ubuntu 7.5.0-6ubuntu2), -O3; the README says C++17, but the Self-Adaptive Hashing Makefile uses --std=c++11 -O3 -g
hardware: Intel Core i9-10980XE @ 3.00GHz (the paper says '36 Intel Core i9-10980XE CPU'), 24.8MiB L3, 128GB DRAM
tradeoffs: A general 'chain rule' framework composing several elementary filters rather than a drop-in single filter; the RocksDB integration is a case study, not a merged patch to upstream RocksDB
caveats: No LICENSE file, so all rights are reserved by default and the code is reference/study-only. The repo says the code is there to help readers understand the paper's algorithms; it is not a packaged library. The headline RocksDB P99 experiment (paper Section 5.4) has no code in the repo, which only covers Algorithms 1-2, the static dictionary, random-access Huffman and self-adaptive Cuckoo hashing. The 36% gain is for existing-key queries at |U|=16M; for non-existing keys at 16M, ChainedFilter latency rises depending on which SSTable reports the false positive. Last commit was 2023-04-27, more than 3 years ago.

name: GBF-NEON (Galois Bipartite Filter, Ribbon-filter variant)
workload: 1M random uint64 keys, queried with 1M positives and 1M negatives on one Apple M2 (src/bench_vs.cpp). GBF is compared with the project's own 64-byte cache-line Blocked Bloom (8 bits set per block) at 8.26 and 12 bits/key, and with a naive Bloom (k=6).
claimed_speedup: 8.4 ns query latency (GBF) vs 16.4 ns (Blocked Bloom, 8.26 bits/key) and 17.6 ns (naive Bloom, k=6) — roughly 2x faster query latency at near-equal memory (8.52 vs 8.26 bits/key), with false positive rate 0.78% vs 2.90%/1.69% (README table, 'Head-to-head vs competent Blocked Bloom').
compiler_and_flags: -O3 -march=native (CMakeLists.txt GBF_BASE_FLAGS), CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; compiler/version not stated
hardware: Apple M2 (Apple Silicon, NEON)
tradeoffs: Static only, no insert/erase after build; build time ~6x slower than Bloom (30ms vs ~4-7ms for 1M keys); no AVX-512 path shipped (x86 falls back to scalar, and author states x86 perf is unverified beyond CI correctness); power-of-2 partition sizing can over-allocate space up to ~30% at adversarial N.
caveats: First-party, self-run benchmark (src/bench_vs.cpp) on an Apple M2. Flags are -O3 -march=native from CMakeLists.txt; the compiler and version are not stated. The Blocked Bloom baseline is the author's own implementation, not an established library. At 1M keys (~1 MB) the filter is cache-resident, and build is ~6x slower than Blocked Bloom (30 vs 5 ms). The README's design-journey note says 8 ideas were tried, 7 failed and 1 shipped. The bench_vs.cpp header still says 'GBF v0.3'. The headline numbers are Apple-M2-only; x86 results exist only in CI artifacts. This is a Ribbon-filter variant, not a novel algorithm, from a brand-new (0-star) single-author project and not independently reproduced.

name: Windowed Cuckoo Filter (WindowFilter, implements 'Smaller and More Flexible Cuckoo Filters')
workload: Bit-packed Bloom filter, standard Cuckoo(2,4) filter, and overlapping-window Cuckoo(2,2) filter compared on bytes/item, false-positive rate, lookup/insert latency, and max load factor
claimed_speedup: Windowed cuckoo (2,2): 1.5958 bytes/item vs Bloom's 1.8034 (README: about 12% less memory) and Cuckoo(2,4)'s 2.1299 (about 25% less) at similar FPR (2^-10 target); lookup 60.28 ns vs Bloom's 81.59 ns and Cuckoo's 61.19 ns (essentially tied with cuckoo). Inserts are slower: 162.97 ns vs 58.74 ns for Cuckoo(2,4) and 93.61 ns for Bloom, and max load is 0.9575 vs 0.9780 for Cuckoo
compiler_and_flags: Rust stable toolchain (version not pinned, rust-toolchain.toml), edition 2024, release profile lto=thin, codegen-units=1
tradeoffs: Insert is slower than both Bloom and plain Cuckoo (162.97 ns vs 93.61 / 58.74 ns) because of the overlapping-window relocation logic
caveats: Third-party Rust reimplementation of arXiv:2505.05847 (Smaller and More Flexible Cuckoo Filters), not the paper authors' code. The baselines are the author's own Bloom and Cuckoo(2,4) implementations, not established libraries. The README table is one run (defaults: 100k items, 200k queries, k=10), with no CPU model and no pinned toolchain version. Inserts are about 2.8x slower than the conventional cuckoo filter. It uses a non-cryptographic hash that is not safe against adversarial input. 0 stars; created and pushed around 2026-09-03.
